data.description: A 57-year-old female without any medical history was admitted for evaluation of a left ventricular tumor that was discovered incidentally. The patient was asymptomatic and had no relevant past medical history. Physical examination findings were not specifically described in the case report.
A rare benign vascular tumor of the heart composed of abnormal blood-filled vascular channels. It may arise in the myocardium, including the left ventricle, and can be incidentally discovered.
symptoms_in_common: Incidentally discovered left ventricular cardiac mass

data.description: A benign primary cardiac tumor composed predominantly of dense fibroblastic and collagenous tissue. It usually occurs in the ventricular myocardium and can be found incidentally, although it is more common in children.
symptoms_in_common: May be asymptomatic when small or nonobstructive
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 57 years, because cardiac fibromas are more commonly diagnosed in infants and children

data.description: The most common benign primary cardiac tumor, usually arising from the interatrial septum in the left atrium. It can cause obstruction, embolic events, or constitutional symptoms, but may occasionally be asymptomatic.
symptoms_not_in_common: Left ventricular location, as myxomas most commonly occur in the left atrium
No embolic symptoms
No constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or fatigue
No symptoms of valvular obstruction or heart failure

data.description: A benign tumor composed of mature adipose tissue that may arise in the subendocardium, myocardium, or pericardium. Many cardiac lipomas are incidentally identified and asymptomatic.
symptoms_not_in_common: Left ventricular myocardial location is less typical than epicardial or right-sided locations
Imaging and gross appearance suggesting a non-fatty, fibrous or vascular lesion rather than a fatty mass

data.description: An intracardiac blood clot, usually associated with atrial fibrillation, ventricular dysfunction, myocardial infarction, ventricular aneurysm, or hypercoagulable states. A left ventricular thrombus typically forms in areas of impaired wall motion.
symptoms_in_common: May be asymptomatic if not embolizing
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of myocardial infarction
No known ventricular dysfunction or aneurysm
No atrial fibrillation or other reported thrombotic risk factor
No embolic manifestations
Appearance described as a tumor rather than a typical mural thrombus

data.description: A previously healthy 10-year-old boy presented with left upper quadrant abdominal pain that worsened with deep breathing or lying down, accompanied by fever. He also complained of mild cough and whitish sputum. On physical examination, the child was irritable but there were no other remarkable findings. Laboratory data showed elevated C-reactive protein (8.65 mg/dL) without leukocytosis and other findings were unremarkable.
Ischemic necrosis of splenic tissue caused by impaired splenic arterial or venous blood flow; imaging commonly shows peripheral wedge-shaped, poorly perfused splenic lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Acute left upper quadrant abdominal pain
Imaging appearance of focal wedge-shaped hypoperfused splenic lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: Mild cough
Whitish sputum

data.diagnosis: Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection with splenic infarction
data.description: A respiratory infection caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae that can rarely produce hypercoagulability, vascular thrombosis, and splenic infarction as extrapulmonary complications.
symptoms_in_common: Absence of marked leukocytosis can occur
Left upper quadrant pain due to possible splenic infarction
Pleuritic worsening of pain with deep breathing
symptoms_not_in_common: No prominent respiratory distress
No reported diffuse pulmonary findings
No reported sore throat or other upper respiratory symptoms

data.description: A localized infection within the spleen, usually bacterial, which can cause fever, inflammatory marker elevation, and left upper quadrant pain; ultrasound may show focal hypoechoic splenic lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Focal splenic abnormality on ultrasound and MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: No leukocytosis
Previously healthy child without known immunodeficiency or bacteremia
Mild cough and whitish sputum are not primary features

data.diagnosis: Community-acquired left lower lobe pneumonia with referred abdominal pain
data.description: Infection of the lower lung can irritate the diaphragm and present with upper abdominal pain, fever, cough, sputum production, and pleuritic pain.
symptoms_in_common: Left upper quadrant pain from diaphragmatic irritation
symptoms_not_in_common: No remarkable chest examination findings reported
No leukocytosis
Focal splenic perfusion abnormalities are not typical of uncomplicated pneumonia

data.description: A 38-year-old woman presented with a three-day history of fever, generalized myalgia and arthralgia, and the sensation of difficulty when breathing in. She had poorly localized discomfort in the left diaphragmatic region on deep inspiration and loose stools over the preceding three days. Three days before presentation she had returned from a three-week trip to Western Australia, and 18 months earlier she had traveled to Vietnam. On examination she appeared well but was febrile at 38.0°C and tachypnoeic at 22 breaths/min, with all other observations normal. Examination of all other systems was unremarkable. Blood tests showed severe neutrophilia (18.9 × 10⁹/L; reference range 2.0-8.1), raised C reactive protein (354 mg/L; reference value <10), and normal renal and liver biochemistry. Chest radiography and urinalysis were normal. Blood cultures taken at presentation were negative.

A hepatic abscess caused by invasive Entamoeba histolytica infection, often occurring weeks to years after travel to an endemic region. It commonly causes fever, leukocytosis, and right upper abdominal or pleuritic diaphragmatic pain; bowel symptoms may be mild or absent.
symptoms_in_common: Marked neutrophilia and elevated C-reactive protein
Pleuritic discomfort in the left diaphragmatic region on deep inspiration
Previous travel to Vietnam, an area where amoebiasis may occur
Normal chest radiograph despite diaphragmatic/pleuritic discomfort
symptoms_not_in_common: Very recent travel to Western Australia is not a typical exposure for amoebic liver abscess
Absence of focal right upper quadrant abdominal pain

data.description: A localized bacterial infection of the liver, commonly caused by enteric organisms such as Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, streptococci, or anaerobes. It produces fever and inflammatory-marker elevation and may cause diaphragmatic pain when located near the liver capsule.
symptoms_in_common: Loose stools, which can accompany an enteric source of infection
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear abdominal tenderness or focal upper abdominal pain on examination
Generalized arthralgia and myalgia are less characteristic than fever and abdominal pain

data.diagnosis: Melioidosis with hepatic abscess (Burkholderia pseudomallei infection)
data.description: Melioidosis is an infection caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, endemic in northern Australia and parts of Southeast Asia. It can cause pneumonia, sepsis, and internal abscesses involving the liver and spleen; incubation may range from days to years.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel to Western Australia and previous travel to Southeast Asia
Marked neutrophilia and elevated C-reactive protein
Possible hepatic abscess on abdominal imaging
Blood cultures can initially be negative
symptoms_not_in_common: No diabetes, chronic kidney disease, hazardous alcohol use, or other stated risk factor for melioidosis
No pulmonary infiltrate on chest radiography
No severe sepsis or hypotension

data.diagnosis: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (perihepatitis associated with pelvic inflammatory disease)
data.description: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is inflammation of the liver capsule, usually caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae in association with pelvic inflammatory disease. It causes sharp pleuritic upper abdominal pain, often with fever.
symptoms_in_common: Pain near the diaphragm that is worse on deep inspiration
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain is left-sided rather than the more typical right upper quadrant pain
No pelvic pain, vaginal discharge, cervical symptoms, or genital examination abnormalities reported
Loose stools are not typical
A focal liver lesion or abscess would not be expected

data.diagnosis: Acute bacterial gastroenteritis with reactive systemic inflammation
data.description: An invasive bacterial intestinal infection, such as Salmonella, Campylobacter, or Shigella infection, can cause fever, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, neutrophilia, and systemic myalgia. Some pathogens can rarely lead to extraintestinal infection including hepatic abscess formation.
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent pleuritic left diaphragmatic pain is not typical of uncomplicated gastroenteritis
No vomiting, significant abdominal cramps, or frequent diarrhoea reported
Tachypnoea and breathing difficulty are not typical of uncomplicated intestinal infection
A liver lesion would suggest a complication rather than simple gastroenteritis

data.description: A 60-year-old white Caucasian woman presented with a 4-year history of worsening gait and sensory disturbance accompanied by urinary urgency and nocturia. She reported slow deterioration in vision from age 50, though she could still drive. Her mother was registered blind and had Parkinson's disease with dementia. On examination, she had a spastic gait with normal power in lower limbs but increased tone and sustained ankle clonus. Reflexes were brisk with flexor plantar responses. She had mild reduction in visual acuity and dyschromatopsia, but no detectable visual field defect and preserved pupillary light reflexes. CSF analysis showed presence of oligoclonal bands. Routine hematological, biochemical and immunological blood tests were normal, including folate and vitamin B12. Anti-aquaporin 4 antibodies were negative in serum.

data.diagnosis: OPA1-related dominant optic atrophy plus syndrome (DOA+)
data.description: A mitochondrial disorder caused by pathogenic OPA1 variants, typically producing slowly progressive bilateral optic atrophy and sometimes additional neurologic features including spastic paraplegia, sensory disturbance, ataxia, neuropathy, deafness, or cognitive impairment.
symptoms_in_common: Slowly progressive visual decline beginning in midlife
Bilateral optic nerve/RNFL thinning consistent with optic atrophy
Increased lower-limb tone, brisk reflexes, and sustained ankle clonus
Urinary urgency and nocturia consistent with upper motor neuron bladder dysfunction
Maternal history of blindness and parkinsonism with dementia, compatible with dominant mitochondrial neurologic disease
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF oligoclonal bands are not a typical defining feature of OPA1-related disease
No hearing loss, ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, or external ophthalmoplegia was reported

data.description: A chronic inflammatory demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system that can cause gradually progressive spastic paraparesis, sensory symptoms, and bladder dysfunction, often with oligoclonal bands in CSF.
symptoms_in_common: Spastic gait with increased tone, brisk reflexes, and sustained ankle clonus
Visual impairment can occur from optic neuritis or optic atrophy
symptoms_not_in_common: Visual decline was slowly progressive over approximately 10 years rather than a typical discrete episode of optic neuritis
Preserved pupillary light reflexes and absence of a visual field defect are less typical of clinically significant prior optic neuritis
The maternal history of blindness with parkinsonism and dementia suggests a possible inherited disorder rather than sporadic multiple sclerosis
The provided brain and spinal imaging does not show typical demyelinating lesion burden

data.diagnosis: Hereditary spastic paraplegia with optic atrophy (complex hereditary spastic paraplegia, including SPG7 or related forms)
data.description: A group of inherited neurodegenerative disorders characterized by progressive lower-limb spasticity; complex forms may also cause optic atrophy, sensory abnormalities, urinary dysfunction, ataxia, neuropathy, and cognitive features.
symptoms_in_common: Normal lower-limb power despite marked upper motor neuron signs
Increased tone, brisk reflexes, and sustained ankle clonus
Slowly progressive optic neuropathy with reduced acuity and color vision impairment
Family history of severe visual and neurologic disease
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF oligoclonal bands are not usually associated with hereditary spastic paraplegia
No ataxia, distal weakness, peripheral neuropathy, or cerebellar signs were reported
The reported maternal pattern may be more suggestive of dominant mitochondrial inheritance than many recessive complex hereditary spastic paraplegias

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder that commonly causes optic neuritis and myelitis, leading to visual loss, sensory symptoms, spasticity, and bladder dysfunction; many cases are associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies.
symptoms_in_common: Spastic gait and upper motor neuron signs
CSF inflammatory markers can occasionally be present
symptoms_not_in_common: Anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies were negative
The course is very slowly progressive rather than characterized by attacks of optic neuritis or transverse myelitis
No painful acute visual loss was reported
No typical longitudinally extensive spinal cord lesion is shown
Bilateral longstanding optic atrophy with a family history of blindness is atypical for NMOSD

data.diagnosis: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with neurologic involvement (LHON-plus)
data.description: A maternally inherited mitochondrial disorder that primarily causes bilateral optic neuropathy and can occasionally be accompanied by movement disorders, peripheral neuropathy, myelopathy, or MS-like neurologic manifestations.
symptoms_in_common: Optic nerve/RNFL thinning compatible with optic atrophy
Maternal family history of severe visual loss
Possible neurologic manifestations including spasticity and sensory symptoms can occur in LHON-plus phenotypes
symptoms_not_in_common: LHON more commonly presents with subacute severe central visual loss in younger adults, often men
The patient's visual decline was gradual and began around age 50
Prominent progressive spastic paraparesis and urinary dysfunction are uncommon in typical LHON
CSF oligoclonal bands are not typical of uncomplicated LHON

data.description: 14-year-old female with over 2 months of generalized pruritus, scleral icterus, and petechiae/ecchymoses on the extremities. She denied fever, abdominal pain, or abdominal distension. Past history included amenorrhea, menstrual irregularities, and acne. She had taken unspecified Chinese herbal medicines for about 9 months. On examination, she was alert with facial acne and pigmentation, mild scleral and mucocutaneous jaundice, a soft non-tender abdomen, and no lower extremity edema.

An autosomal-recessive ATP7B disorder causing impaired biliary copper excretion, copper accumulation in the liver, brain, and cornea, and progressive hepatic, neurologic, hematologic, and endocrine manifestations.
symptoms_in_common: Petechiae and ecchymoses, which may reflect liver-related coagulopathy or thrombocytopenia
Basal ganglia MRI abnormalities compatible with copper deposition
Corneal findings compatible with Kayser-Fleischer rings
symptoms_not_in_common: No abdominal pain
No abdominal distension
No lower-extremity edema
No reported neurologic symptoms such as tremor, dysarthria, dystonia, or behavioral change

data.diagnosis: Herb-induced liver injury with cholestatic hepatitis
data.description: Liver injury caused by herbal or traditional medicines, often presenting with cholestasis, jaundice, pruritus, and sometimes impaired hepatic synthetic function.
symptoms_in_common: Use of unspecified Chinese herbal medicines for approximately 9 months
Petechiae and ecchymoses, potentially due to liver dysfunction and impaired coagulation
Absence of fever and abdominal tenderness
symptoms_not_in_common: Basal ganglia MRI changes suggestive of metal deposition
Corneal findings compatible with Kayser-Fleischer rings
Pathogenic homozygous ATP7B mutation
Amenorrhea and menstrual irregularities are not typical primary manifestations of acute herb-induced cholestatic injury

data.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease that can occur in children and adolescents and may lead to jaundice, chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, and impaired liver synthetic function.
symptoms_in_common: Petechiae and ecchymoses that could occur with significant liver dysfunction
Menstrual irregularities can occur in chronic liver disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent generalized pruritus is less typical unless there is substantial cholestasis
Long-term Chinese herbal medicine exposure does not specifically support autoimmune hepatitis
Basal ganglia MRI changes compatible with copper deposition
Corneal Kayser-Fleischer-type findings
Homozygous pathogenic ATP7B mutation

data.diagnosis: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis or other inherited cholestatic liver disease
data.description: A group of genetic disorders causing impaired bile formation or transport, leading to childhood or adolescent cholestasis, severe pruritus, jaundice, and progressive liver disease.
symptoms_in_common: Possible petechiae and ecchymoses if advanced liver dysfunction causes coagulopathy
symptoms_not_in_common: Basal ganglia MRI abnormalities suggesting metal deposition
Corneal Kayser-Fleischer-type findings
Homozygous ATP7B pathogenic variant specifically supports Wilson disease rather than PFIC
Menstrual irregularities and acne are not characteristic presenting features
Chinese herbal medicine exposure is not a typical cause

data.description: 66-year-old man with a 2-day history of fever, lethargy, polyarticular arthralgias, and a painful rash. Past history: hypertension, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, and biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis; azathioprine 75 mg had been started 10 days earlier. On examination, temperature was 38°C with bilateral tender knees and a patellar tap. Labs showed mild leukocytosis with neutrophilia, elevated CRP and ESR, slightly elevated rheumatoid factor, and negative anti-CCP, ANA-related tests, anti-dsDNA, and anti-ASO. Renal function and urinalysis were normal, chest radiograph was normal, and synovial fluid was noninflammatory with no bacteria or crystals.

An acute systemic drug-hypersensitivity reaction to azathioprine, typically occurring within days to weeks of starting treatment and causing fever, malaise, rash, arthralgia, and inflammatory-marker elevation.
symptoms_in_common: Symptoms began 10 days after starting azathioprine
symptoms_not_in_common: No clear atypical symptoms; renal function and urinalysis are normal, which helps exclude organ-involving drug reactions

data.diagnosis: Drug-induced Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis)
data.description: A neutrophilic inflammatory skin disorder that may be triggered by medications, including azathioprine, and commonly presents with fever, painful erythematous plaques or nodules, arthralgia, and neutrophilia.
symptoms_in_common: Painful red skin lesions or plaques
Temporal association with a newly started medication
symptoms_not_in_common: Knee joint effusions are less characteristic than skin and systemic manifestations
Synovial fluid is noninflammatory
No skin-biopsy finding of dense neutrophilic infiltration is provided

data.diagnosis: Serum sickness-like reaction due to azathioprine
data.description: A medication-related immune reaction characterized by fever, rash, malaise, and polyarthralgia, usually arising one to two weeks after exposure to a new drug.
symptoms_in_common: Onset approximately 10 days after exposure to azathioprine
symptoms_not_in_common: Neutrophilic leukocytosis is not a defining feature
The rash appears more plaque-like and painful rather than the typical urticarial eruption
No edema, lymphadenopathy, or complement abnormalities are reported

data.description: An inflammatory panniculitis causing painful erythematous nodules, usually on the lower legs, often accompanied by fever, arthralgia, and elevated inflammatory markers; it can be triggered by drugs, infection, or autoimmune disease.
symptoms_in_common: Painful erythematous lesions on the legs
symptoms_not_in_common: The rash distribution and morphology are not clearly typical of tender subcutaneous shin nodules
Neutrophilic leukocytosis is nonspecific
The close timing after azathioprine initiation favors a drug-hypersensitivity syndrome instead

data.description: A 60-year-old woman presented after sustaining direct trauma to the anterior neck from a fall. She developed progressively worsening hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing, and pain with neck movement. Physical examination revealed visible neck swelling with bruising tracking onto the anterior chest wall. There was no tenderness on palpation of the cervical spine. On flexible nasal endoscopy, swelling of the posterior pharyngeal wall was observed, indicating potential airway compromise.
Bleeding into the retropharyngeal/prevertebral soft tissues after neck trauma, which can expand and compress the pharynx and upper airway.
symptoms_in_common: Bruising extending onto the anterior chest wall
Posterior pharyngeal wall swelling on flexible endoscopy

data.diagnosis: Blunt laryngeal trauma with laryngeal edema or hematoma
data.description: Injury to the larynx after blunt anterior neck trauma, causing soft-tissue swelling, vocal-cord dysfunction, hematoma, and possible airway obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Direct trauma to the anterior neck
symptoms_not_in_common: Posterior pharyngeal wall swelling is more suggestive of a retropharyngeal process than an isolated laryngeal injury
Bruising tracking onto the anterior chest wall is not specific for isolated laryngeal trauma

data.diagnosis: Cervical spine injury with associated prevertebral soft-tissue hematoma
data.description: A cervical vertebral fracture or ligamentous injury may cause bleeding and swelling in the prevertebral/retropharyngeal space, sometimes producing dysphagia and airway compression.
symptoms_not_in_common: No cervical spine tenderness on examination
Hoarse voice is less typical unless there is substantial associated retropharyngeal or laryngeal swelling
Visible anterior neck bruising and chest-wall bruising may occur without a cervical spine injury

data.description: 37-year-old man with 3 months of recurrent episodes of weakness, irritability, poor concentration, sweet cravings, confusion/foggy sensorium, cold clamminess, and fatigue, usually after several hours without eating and worse at night or early morning. Wife noted abnormal behavior and prolonged memory loss. He gained 30 lb after drinking large amounts of cola for symptom relief. No significant past medical history aside from prior umbilical hernia repair and back surgery; no medications. On examination he was confused, cold, and clammy; other systems were unremarkable. Routine labs, HbA1c, adrenal testing, calcium, and pituitary hormones were normal except mildly elevated prolactin. During evaluation, glucose was 2.4 mmol/L with inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide. Imaging showed a 1.8 × 1.3 cm hypervascular lesion between the head and neck of the pancreas.

A usually benign pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that autonomously secretes insulin, causing recurrent fasting hypoglycemia. It classically produces Whipple triad: symptoms of hypoglycemia, low measured glucose, and improvement after glucose intake.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent episodes after several hours without eating
Symptoms worse at night or early morning
Sweet cravings and symptom relief with cola
Weight gain from frequent carbohydrate intake
symptoms_not_in_common: Mildly elevated prolactin is not a typical direct manifestation of an isolated insulinoma

data.description: A biochemical syndrome of hypoglycemia caused by inappropriate internal insulin secretion, most commonly due to insulinoma, but potentially due to other causes such as diffuse beta-cell hyperfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Weight gain due to frequent carbohydrate consumption
symptoms_not_in_common: A discrete hypervascular pancreatic mass suggests a specific insulinoma rather than the broader syndrome alone
Mild prolactin elevation is not characteristic

data.description: Diffuse pancreatic beta-cell hyperfunction causing excessive insulin release and hypoglycemia. In adults it is less common than insulinoma and may occur after gastrointestinal surgery, though it can be idiopathic.
symptoms_in_common: Low glucose with elevated insulin and C-peptide
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms are primarily fasting/nocturnal rather than predominantly postprandial
No history of bariatric or gastric surgery
A focal 1.8 cm hypervascular pancreatic lesion is more typical of insulinoma than diffuse beta-cell hyperplasia
Weight gain is not a defining feature

data.diagnosis: Factitious hypoglycemia due to sulfonylurea or meglitinide exposure
data.description: Hypoglycemia caused by ingestion of insulin-secretagogue medications, which stimulate endogenous pancreatic insulin release and therefore produce elevated insulin and C-peptide levels.
symptoms_in_common: Fasting or nocturnal symptoms can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: He reports no medication use
A hypervascular pancreatic lesion is not expected
The persistent pattern over several months with pancreatic mass strongly favors insulinoma
No evidence of access to diabetes medications is provided

data.description: Hypoglycemia caused by administration of insulin from an external source, either accidental or intentional. Laboratory testing typically shows high insulin with suppressed endogenous C-peptide.
symptoms_not_in_common: C-peptide is elevated rather than suppressed
No insulin use or diabetes history is reported
The pancreatic hypervascular lesion is not explained by exogenous insulin use
Weight gain from compensatory cola intake is possible but not specific

data.description: Deficient cortisol production, due to adrenal or pituitary disease, which can impair glucose maintenance and cause fatigue, weakness, and sometimes hypoglycemia.
symptoms_not_in_common: Adrenal testing was normal
Insulin and C-peptide are inappropriately elevated, which is not expected
Cold clamminess and neuroglycopenic episodes are better explained by hyperinsulinemia
No hypotension, hyperpigmentation, abdominal symptoms, salt craving, or electrolyte abnormalities are described
Hypervascular pancreatic lesion is not explained

data.description: A 39-year-old male, with no prior relevant medical history, presents with atraumatic intermittent sharp pain in the lower segment of the right anterior thoracic wall. The symptoms began two months earlier when the patient started exercising (CrossFit), mostly triggered by training (especially abdominal crunches) whilst being asymptomatic in normal daily activities.

data.diagnosis: Slipping rib syndrome (interchondral subluxation of a false rib)
data.description: Hypermobility or subluxation of the anterior cartilaginous portion of a lower false rib, usually ribs 8-10, causing intermittent sharp lower chest or upper abdominal wall pain from intercostal nerve irritation. Dynamic ultrasound may demonstrate abnormal movement of the involved rib cartilage.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent sharp pain in the lower anterior thoracic wall
Pain provoked by exercise and trunk movement
Pain particularly triggered by abdominal crunches
Minimal or absent symptoms during ordinary daily activities

data.description: Overuse or partial injury of the muscles between the ribs, often following new or intense exercise, twisting, forceful breathing, or core training.
symptoms_in_common: Atraumatic pain beginning after initiation of CrossFit
Pain brought on by training and abdominal exercises
Absence of symptoms during routine daily activity
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent lower-rib symptoms specifically associated with possible rib-cartilage movement are more suggestive of slipping rib syndrome

data.description: Inflammation or irritation of costochondral or chondrosternal junctions that causes localized chest-wall pain, often worsened by movement, deep inspiration, or palpation.
symptoms_in_common: Pain provoked by physical exertion and chest-wall movement
No reported systemic illness or prior major medical history
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain is located in the lower anterior chest wall rather than the more typical upper costochondral junctions
Intermittent pain specifically provoked by crunches is less typical
No tenderness to palpation, swelling, or pain with normal activity is reported

data.diagnosis: Rib stress injury or stress fracture
data.description: A repetitive-load injury to a rib that can occur in athletes after a sudden increase in training volume or intensity, producing focal pain that worsens with activity.
symptoms_in_common: Recent initiation of intensive CrossFit exercise
symptoms_not_in_common: No persistent pain at rest is reported
No reported focal bony tenderness
No pain with normal daily activities is reported
Intermittent movement-related symptoms favor a hypermobile rib/cartilage process over a stress fracture

data.diagnosis: Abdominal rectus or external oblique muscle strain
data.description: Overuse injury of the anterior abdominal-wall musculature, commonly associated with forceful trunk flexion, rotation, or high-intensity core exercises.
symptoms_in_common: Pain is especially triggered by abdominal crunches
Pain is absent during normal daily activities
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain is described as being in the lower anterior thoracic wall rather than primarily the abdominal wall
Lower-rib localization and suspected rib-cartilage abnormality are less typical for an isolated abdominal muscle strain

data.description: A 31-year-old woman underwent barium enema examination as part of a medical checkup. She had been healthy without specific complaints and had no significant past medical or family history. The patient was 161 cm in height and weighed 44 kg, appeared well, and the physical examination showed no abnormalities. Complete blood cell count and biochemical analysis of the blood for hepatic and renal function, urine analysis, and fecal occult blood test were all within normal limits. The tumor markers for CEA and CA 19-9 were also normal. No lesions were observed on the upper endoscopy and the abdominal ultrasound.

67-year-old previously healthy male with 4 months of dry cough, wheezing, and mild dyspnea, worsening despite inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids after prior diagnosis of eosinophilic asthma. No smoking history or significant medical history. On examination, he required 1 L/min nasal oxygen, had decreased breath sounds and fine crackles in the right lower lung field, with no jugular venous distension, murmurs, gallop, or peripheral edema. Chest x-ray showed right-sided ground-glass opacities, and high-resolution CT revealed ground-glass opacities with surrounding consolidation in the right lower lung field. Labs showed marked eosinophilia, elevated CRP, and mild anemia.

data.diagnosis: Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, not otherwise specified (CEL-NOS)
data.description: A clonal myeloid neoplasm characterized by persistent marked eosinophilia, abnormal eosinophil precursors or blasts, dysplastic hematopoiesis, and often cytogenetic abnormalities. It can cause pulmonary eosinophilic infiltration and respiratory symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Right lower-lung ground-glass opacities with surrounding consolidation
Abnormal eosinophil maturation and dysplastic myeloid cells on peripheral smear
Poor response to inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids
symptoms_not_in_common: Prior diagnosis of eosinophilic asthma
Absence of constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats

data.diagnosis: Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and tyrosine-kinase gene rearrangement (such as PDGFRA, PDGFRB, FGFR1, or PCM1-JAK2 rearrangement)
data.description: A group of clonal hematologic neoplasms in which a kinase-gene rearrangement drives eosinophil proliferation. These disorders may involve blood, bone marrow, lungs, skin, heart, or other organs and can mimic allergic asthma or eosinophilic pneumonia.
symptoms_in_common: Respiratory symptoms including cough, wheezing, and dyspnea
Pulmonary infiltrates with ground-glass opacity and consolidation
Failure of standard inhaled asthma treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported splenomegaly
No reported hepatomegaly
No reported skin, cardiac, neurologic, or gastrointestinal involvement

data.description: An eosinophilic lung disease causing subacute cough, dyspnea, blood eosinophilia, and pulmonary opacities due to eosinophil accumulation in lung tissue. It is often associated with asthma but generally responds dramatically to systemic corticosteroids.
symptoms_in_common: Four months of subacute respiratory symptoms
symptoms_not_in_common: Unilateral right lower-lung predominance rather than the more typical bilateral peripheral upper-lung infiltrates
Abnormal eosinophil precursors and dysplastic myeloid cells on blood smear
Mild anemia suggesting possible bone-marrow disease
Poor response to corticosteroid-containing inhaler therapy

data.description: A systemic eosinophilic vasculitis usually associated with adult-onset asthma, eosinophilia, sinus disease, pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy, skin lesions, and possible cardiac or renal involvement.
symptoms_not_in_common: No chronic sinusitis or nasal polyps reported
No peripheral neuropathy reported
No rash or purpura reported
No renal disease reported
No cardiac manifestations reported
Dysplastic eosinophil precursors and cytogenetic abnormalities would be atypical for vasculitis

data.description: A 12-year-old boy presented with a 1-month history of malaise, fevers, abdominal pain, and worsening pallor. His symptoms began with headache and abdominal pain, with an initial temperature of 38.6°C and pale skin. He experienced persistent upper abdominal pain and recurrent fevers. The patient reported nausea, occasional diarrhea, headache, myalgias, fatigue, and occasional dizziness. He described nearly constant periumbilical pain radiating to the left lower quadrant, with occasional blood in stools. His height was 132 cm (1st percentile), weight 26.8 kg (1st percentile), with recent 1 kg weight loss. Physical examination revealed pale skin and mucosa, distended abdomen with mild tenderness in right upper and left lower quadrants, and ecchymoses on the shins. He had visited the Dominican Republic 3 months prior. Laboratory tests showed severe microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 6.7 g/dL), elevated inflammatory markers (ESR >140 mm/hr, CRP 143.2 mg/liter), and elevated ferritin (320 μg/L).

An aggressive CD30-positive T-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that commonly occurs in children and may cause systemic symptoms, lymphadenopathy, extranodal abdominal disease, and inflammatory laboratory abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Possible bowel involvement causing diarrhea and blood in stools
symptoms_not_in_common: Recent travel to the Dominican Republic
Microcytic anemia specifically, which more strongly suggests iron deficiency or chronic gastrointestinal blood loss
Nearly constant periumbilical pain radiating to the left lower quadrant

data.description: A B-cell lymphoma characterized by inflammatory symptoms and often painless lymph-node enlargement; advanced disease can produce constitutional symptoms, anemia, and extranodal involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Abdominal discomfort from intra-abdominal lymphadenopathy or organ involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Occasional bloody stools
Diarrhea
Marked microcytic anemia from apparent gastrointestinal blood loss
Persistent focal periumbilical and left-lower-quadrant abdominal pain
Recent travel to the Dominican Republic

data.description: A rapidly growing high-grade B-cell lymphoma in children that frequently involves the abdomen, particularly the ileocecal region, and may cause bowel symptoms, bleeding, obstruction, and systemic illness.
symptoms_in_common: Possible intra-abdominal mass or lymph-node disease
symptoms_not_in_common: One-month relatively gradual course, since Burkitt lymphoma often progresses very rapidly
Recurrent fever as the predominant early feature
Recent travel to the Dominican Republic

data.description: A chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract and commonly causes abdominal pain, diarrhea, gastrointestinal bleeding, growth failure, inflammation, and iron-deficiency anemia in children.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic periumbilical and left-lower-quadrant abdominal pain
Height and weight at the 1st percentile, suggesting poor growth
Severe microcytic anemia consistent with iron deficiency from intestinal inflammation or bleeding
Elevated ferritin as an acute-phase reactant
symptoms_not_in_common: Ecchymoses on the shins
Very high recurrent fevers may be more suggestive of severe infection, abscess, or malignancy
Imaging concern for widespread nodal or extranodal lesions would be atypical for uncomplicated Crohn disease
Recent travel to the Dominican Republic is not required for Crohn disease

data.description: A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma species, which can occur after exposure in endemic areas and may cause prolonged fever, weight loss, anemia, abdominal symptoms, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenic involvement, and elevated inflammatory markers.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel to the Dominican Republic, an area where Histoplasma exposure can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe microcytic anemia, which is less characteristic than anemia of inflammation or pancytopenia
Occasional bloody stools
Ecchymoses without reported thrombocytopenia
No reported respiratory symptoms despite possible disseminated fungal infection

diagnoses.title: Mixed cellularity classical Hodgkin lymphoma

data.description: 39-year-old man presented with 4 days of fever with shaking chills, diffuse headache, fatigue, lower back pain, weakness, anorexia, decreased urine output with dark urine, and blurry vision during fever episodes after returning from a 2-week trip to East Africa. During travel in Tanzania, he had mosquito bites and ate cooked seafood and a small amount of raw tuna; 2 days before returning, he developed nausea, vomiting, and nonbloody diarrhea. Past history included degenerative knee disease with prior glucocorticoid injections. On examination, he was febrile, flushed, with mild scleral icterus and dark brown urine. Initial labs showed thrombocytopenia, elevated creatinine, elevated AST/ALT, hyperbilirubinemia, and low haptoglobin.

Severe mosquito-borne malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum, which can produce high parasitemia, intravascular hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury, jaundice, and multiorgan dysfunction. The travel history, malaria rapid test, and blood smear showing ring forms are highly supportive.
symptoms_in_common: Fever with shaking chills after travel to Tanzania
Dark brown urine consistent with hemoglobinuria from hemolysis
Elevated creatinine consistent with acute kidney injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Lower back pain is less specific but can occur with severe hemolysis
Recent raw tuna and cooked seafood exposure are not typical transmission routes

data.diagnosis: Severe falciparum malaria with blackwater fever
data.description: A severe hemolytic manifestation of falciparum malaria characterized by massive intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria causing dark urine, jaundice, and potentially acute renal failure.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel to a falciparum-malaria-endemic region
symptoms_not_in_common: Diarrhea is not a defining feature
Blurry vision is not a classic feature
Raw seafood exposure is unrelated

data.description: A zoonotic spirochetal infection acquired through exposure to water or soil contaminated with animal urine. Severe disease can cause fever, headache, jaundice, acute kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, and dark urine.
symptoms_not_in_common: Mosquito bites are not the usual route of transmission
Low haptoglobin due to marked intravascular hemolysis is less typical
Blood smear with intraerythrocytic malaria parasites would not be explained
No reported freshwater, floodwater, rodent, or animal-urine exposure

data.description: A mosquito-borne viral illness that commonly causes high fever, headache, gastrointestinal symptoms, thrombocytopenia, and elevated liver enzymes. Severe dengue can cause plasma leakage, bleeding, and organ dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Travel to East Africa with mosquito exposure
Decreased urine output in severe illness
symptoms_not_in_common: Dark brown urine from hemoglobinuria is not typical
Low haptoglobin and prominent hemolysis are not typical
Jaundice is less common
Malaria rapid-test positivity and intraerythrocytic ring forms would not be explained
No rash, severe myalgias, mucosal bleeding, or hemorrhagic manifestations were reported

data.diagnosis: Acute viral hepatitis A or E
data.description: Food- and water-associated viral hepatitis causing fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, jaundice, dark urine, and elevated aminotransferases. Hepatitis E is particularly relevant after travel to endemic regions.
symptoms_not_in_common: Shaking chills are less characteristic
Thrombocytopenia is not usually prominent
Low haptoglobin indicating hemolysis is not typical
Acute kidney injury with oliguria is less typical in uncomplicated viral hepatitis
Mosquito exposure is unrelated
Blood smear findings of malaria would not be explained

data.description: 24-year-old male with quadriplegia from a car accident 5 years prior that required cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. Presented with dysphagia, odynophagia, neck pain, fever, and chills. Medical history significant for quadriplegia requiring cervical spine stabilization with metal plates. CT and MRI showed large paraspinal abscess extending from cervical spine 4 to thoracic spine 11.

data.diagnosis: Delayed esophageal perforation from cervical spine hardware erosion
data.description: A late complication of anterior cervical spine fixation in which plates or screws erode into or perforate the pharynx/esophagus, causing leakage, infection, and possible fistula formation.
symptoms_in_common: History of cervical spine stabilization with metal plates
Endoscopic appearance consistent with exposed or eroding cervical hardware
symptoms_not_in_common: Quadriplegia from prior trauma
Abscess extending as far as thoracic vertebra 11

data.description: A severe infection of the mediastinum that spreads downward from a neck, pharyngeal, esophageal, or cervical-spine source and can produce pus collections in the chest.
symptoms_in_common: Infection extending from the cervical region into the thoracic region
symptoms_not_in_common: Quadriplegia
Remote cervical spine stabilization with metal plates is not required for this condition

data.diagnosis: Cervical spinal instrumentation infection with paraspinal abscess
data.description: Infection involving prior cervical fusion hardware and surrounding soft tissues, producing a deep paraspinal abscess that may spread into the retropharyngeal space, esophagus, or mediastinum.
symptoms_in_common: Large cervical-to-thoracic paraspinal abscess on CT and MRI
Dysphagia due to mass effect or adjacent inflammatory involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: Odynophagia is less typical unless there is pharyngeal or esophageal involvement
Quadriplegia itself is not a symptom of the active infection

data.description: A collection of pus in the deep fascial spaces of the neck that can cause painful swallowing and may extend into the mediastinum through the danger space.
symptoms_in_common: Potential spread from the neck into the thoracic mediastinum
symptoms_not_in_common: Paraspinal abscess extending to thoracic vertebra 11 is unusually extensive
Prior cervical hardware erosion would indicate a more specific underlying cause
Quadriplegia

data.diagnosis: Esophagomediastinal fistula secondary to infected cervical hardware
data.description: An abnormal communication between the esophagus and mediastinal infected space, often caused by perforation from cervical instrumentation, allowing saliva and bacteria to contaminate the mediastinum.
symptoms_in_common: Evidence of mediastinal pus near the upper esophagus
symptoms_not_in_common: Quadriplegia
Neck pain is possible but not specific for a fistula

data.description: A 58-year-old male with worsening nausea for the past 72 hours presented to the emergency department with severe chest pain radiating to the back in the context of 4 recent episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious emesis. He was afebrile, diaphoretic, and mildly tachycardic. Cardiac workup, complete blood count, and electrolytes were normal.

A full-thickness rupture of the esophagus, usually in the distal left posterolateral esophagus, caused by a sudden increase in intrathoracic pressure after forceful vomiting. It causes mediastinal air, pleural contamination, and may rapidly progress to sepsis.
symptoms_in_common: Severe chest pain following repeated episodes of vomiting
Chest pain radiating to the back
Pleural fluid collections and left-sided hydropneumothorax/pleural effusion on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Afebrile presentation
Normal complete blood count
Normal electrolytes

data.description: A mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction caused by retching or vomiting, typically producing upper gastrointestinal bleeding rather than a full-thickness esophageal perforation.
symptoms_in_common: Chest or upper abdominal discomfort may occur after retching
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe chest pain radiating to the back
Diaphoresis and tachycardia without bleeding
Non-bloody emesis
Pneumomediastinum on imaging
Pleural effusion or hydropneumothorax on imaging
No hematemesis

data.description: Myocardial ischemia caused by reduced coronary blood flow, commonly presenting with pressure-like chest pain, diaphoresis, nausea, and vomiting.
symptoms_in_common: Age and sex are compatible with increased cardiovascular risk
symptoms_not_in_common: Chest pain beginning after repeated vomiting
Pain radiating to the back rather than typical arm, jaw, or neck radiation
Normal cardiac workup
Pneumomediastinum on imaging
Pleural air/fluid collections consistent with thoracic contamination

data.description: A tear in the aortic intima allowing blood to dissect through the aortic wall, often causing abrupt severe tearing chest pain that radiates to the back.
symptoms_in_common: Severe chest pain radiating to the back
Nausea and vomiting can accompany severe pain
symptoms_not_in_common: Pain occurring in the setting of repeated emesis
Pneumomediastinum on imaging
Hydropneumothorax or pleural contamination pattern on imaging
No reported pulse deficit, neurologic deficit, hypotension, or aortic imaging abnormality
Normal cardiac workup does not establish aortic dissection but supports an alternative cause of chest pain

data.description: 27-year-old man with 2-year history of recurrent convulsive episodes. Initial events involved shaking of the trunk and limbs lasting 4–5 minutes, preceded by occipital headache radiating to the neck, blurred vision, palpitations, nausea, and difficulty concentrating. Four months before admission, he had an episode with sudden body stiffening, fall, shaking for 5–8 minutes, and urinary incontinence. Despite levetiracetam, seizures continued about weekly; one month before admission, he was found on the floor with shaking and clenching movements lasting about 2 minutes. On examination, he was awake and alert but nonverbal, with a stiff posture and intermittent nonrhythmic tremulous movements of the trunk and limbs, and extensive burn scars on the face, trunk, back, arms, and legs. Past history included childhood febrile seizure, several concussions, asthma, major depressive disorder, chronic PTSD, and panic disorder with agoraphobia. Labs showed normal glucose, electrolytes, liver and kidney function, with mildly elevated lactate and creatine kinase.

Paroxysmal episodes that resemble epileptic seizures but are not caused by epileptic cortical discharges; they are commonly associated with psychological trauma, PTSD, depression, anxiety, and other functional neurologic symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Episodes lasting several minutes, including 5–8 minutes
Stiff posture with preserved wakefulness and alertness
Chronic PTSD, major depressive disorder, panic disorder, and agoraphobia
History of trauma suggested by extensive burn scars
symptoms_not_in_common: Urinary incontinence during one event
Childhood febrile seizure history
Mildly elevated creatine kinase and lactate after events
Sudden fall with apparent generalized stiffening

data.description: Epileptic seizures characterized by abrupt loss of consciousness, tonic stiffening followed by rhythmic clonic jerking, and a postictal recovery period. They may be primary generalized or focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
symptoms_in_common: Shaking of the trunk and limbs
Mild elevation of lactate and creatine kinase after convulsive activity
History of multiple concussions, which may increase risk of epilepsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Events continuing despite antiseizure treatment
Prolonged and variable episode durations
Intermittent nonrhythmic tremulous movements rather than consistently rhythmic clonic jerking
Awake and alert but nonverbal stiff state between or during apparent motor activity
Strong psychiatric trauma history that raises concern for functional seizures

data.diagnosis: Focal epilepsy with focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures
data.description: Seizures beginning in one brain region, sometimes with an aura, that spread to produce bilateral tonic-clonic convulsions. Focal seizures can be associated with sensory, visual, autonomic, cognitive, or emotional symptoms before convulsions.
symptoms_in_common: Possible pre-event aura with occipital headache, blurred vision, nausea, palpitations, and difficulty concentrating
Progression from warning symptoms to generalized shaking
Sudden stiffening followed by convulsive movements
History of repeated concussions, which can be associated with post-traumatic focal epilepsy
symptoms_not_in_common: Very prolonged convulsive durations of 4–8 minutes without clear description of prolonged postictal impairment
Nonrhythmic tremulous movements observed while awake and alert
Marked variability among episodes
Persistence of frequent events despite levetiracetam
Psychiatric comorbidity and trauma history that may better support functional seizures

data.description: Transient loss of consciousness caused by reduced cerebral blood flow, often due to vasovagal episodes or cardiac arrhythmia. Brief tonic or myoclonic jerks can occur during syncope and may mimic epilepsy.
symptoms_in_common: Nausea and blurred vision before events
Brief shaking or clenching movements can occur with syncope
Episodes may be mistaken for seizures
symptoms_not_in_common: Repeated convulsive activity lasting 4–8 minutes
Urinary incontinence is less typical
Recurrent prolonged nonrhythmic tremulous movements while awake
No reported clear fainting trigger, pallor, or rapid recovery after loss of consciousness
Mild creatine kinase elevation suggesting substantial muscle activity

data.description: 92-year-old woman with BMI 14.2 kg/m². Past history: no abdominal surgery, five children by normal vaginal delivery. Presenting with: 2-day history of sudden onset right knee pain, 1-day history of nausea and vomiting. Physical exam: no knee swelling/tenderness, patient frequently flexed right knee for pain relief, abdominal distension present, tenderness to deep palpation but no peritoneal irritation signs, no abdominal mass. Rectal exam revealed small extraluminal mass on right side. Initial abdominal radiograph showed small-bowel obstruction.

data.diagnosis: Incarcerated right obturator hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
data.description: A pelvic hernia in which small bowel protrudes through the obturator canal. It classically occurs in thin, elderly, multiparous women and may cause bowel obstruction with pain radiating to the medial thigh or knee (Howship-Romberg sign).
symptoms_in_common: History of multiple pregnancies and vaginal deliveries
Acute small-bowel obstruction on abdominal radiograph
Deep abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs
Sudden right knee pain without local knee swelling or tenderness
Flexing the right knee for pain relief
Right-sided extraluminal mass on rectal examination

data.diagnosis: Incarcerated femoral hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
data.description: A femoral hernia occurs when bowel passes through the femoral canal below the inguinal ligament. It is more common in older women and can become incarcerated or strangulated, causing bowel obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: No prior abdominal surgery, making hernia a possible cause of obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden isolated right knee pain
Relief of pain by flexing the right knee
No groin or upper-thigh mass described
Right-sided extraluminal mass detected on rectal examination rather than a palpable femoral mass

data.diagnosis: Incarcerated inguinal hernia causing small-bowel obstruction
data.description: An inguinal hernia is protrusion of abdominal contents through the inguinal canal. If bowel becomes trapped, it may cause acute intestinal obstruction and potentially ischemia.
symptoms_not_in_common: Very thin elderly multiparous woman is more characteristic of obturator hernia than inguinal hernia
Sudden right knee pain without local knee findings
Pain relieved by flexion of the right knee
No palpable inguinal mass reported
Right-sided pelvic extraluminal mass on rectal examination

data.description: 23-year-old Korean female with 6 months of recurrent bilateral visual field defects and headache, worsened 1 month before presentation. She presented with 1 day of left-eye visual disturbance and left visual field defect, then developed sudden left-sided hearing loss 2 days later. Three weeks after initial presentation, she reported right-eye visual field defect, and 2 days later was admitted for tinnitus, severe headache, and arm numbness. She denied diabetes, hypertension, connective tissue disease, tuberculosis, hematologic disease, cardiovascular disease, oral contraceptive use, and pregnancy. Initial exam showed reactive pupils without relative afferent pupillary defect, corrected visual acuity 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye, normal intraocular pressure bilaterally, and normal anterior segment examination. Laboratory studies including lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibody, ESR, and CRP were normal; CSF showed mildly elevated protein (74.4 mg/dL) without oligoclonal bands. No specific hematologic or rheumatologic abnormalities were found.

A rare autoimmune endotheliopathy causing microvascular occlusion in the brain, retina, and inner ear. It classically presents with encephalopathy or headache, branch retinal artery occlusions, and sensorineural hearing loss; corpus callosum lesions are characteristic on MRI.
symptoms_in_common: Young woman with severe recurrent headache
Retinal arterial occlusion/retinal ischemic changes suggested by fundus photography and fluorescein angiography
Mildly elevated CSF protein without oligoclonal bands
MRI brain lesions involving the corpus callosum/periventricular region
Normal inflammatory, rheumatologic, and thrombophilia testing
symptoms_not_in_common: Preserved central visual acuity despite visual field loss is possible but not the most prominent presentation
No overt encephalopathy, confusion, or cognitive decline was reported

data.description: An immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that commonly affects young women and can cause recurrent neurologic deficits, optic neuritis, sensory symptoms, and characteristic white-matter MRI lesions.
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is uncommon
Tinnitus is not a typical major manifestation
Retinal branch arterial occlusion is not typical of multiple sclerosis
Fluorescein angiographic retinal arterial ischemia is not typical
CSF lacked oligoclonal bands
Visual field defects occurred without typical painful optic neuritis or relative afferent pupillary defect

data.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus with retinal vasculopathy/antiphospholipid-associated retinal vascular occlusion
data.description: Systemic autoimmune disease and/or antiphospholipid syndrome can cause arterial thrombosis, retinal vascular occlusions, central nervous system ischemia, headache, and neurologic symptoms in young women.
symptoms_in_common: Focal neurologic symptom of arm numbness
symptoms_not_in_common: Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibody tests were normal
No connective-tissue disease history or systemic lupus features were reported
ESR and CRP were normal
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus are less typical
No hematologic abnormalities were found
Corpus callosum lesion pattern together with retinal and cochlear involvement is more characteristic of Susac syndrome

data.description: Behçet disease is a systemic inflammatory vasculitis that may cause recurrent ocular inflammation and retinal vascular disease, neurologic involvement, headache, and occasionally auditory symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Visual field defects associated with retinal vascular abnormalities
Possible central nervous system lesion on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: No recurrent oral ulcers were reported
No genital ulcers, skin lesions, arthritis, or uveitis were reported
Anterior segment examination was normal
Retinal arterial occlusion without inflammatory ocular findings is less typical
Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is not a classic feature
Normal inflammatory markers make active systemic vasculitis less likely

data.description: 73-year-old woman with a 10-year history of progressive paraspinal muscle atrophy and cerebellar ataxia. Symptoms began at age 63 with slight stooping posture, later progressing to gait instability requiring a walking stick by age 68 and difficulty climbing stairs by age 70. Exam showed moderate neck flexion weakness, mild proximal limb weakness, poor tandem gait balance without limb ataxia, and MMSE score 25. Labs showed elevated creatine kinase, normal lactate, slightly low TSH, elevated antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibodies, elevated rheumatoid factor, and mildly positive ANA. EMG showed mild myopathic changes. Audiometry revealed sensorineural high-frequency hearing loss, and Holter monitoring showed frequent premature contractions.

A hereditary muscle disease caused by disruption of myofibrillar structural proteins, often including desmin. It can produce progressive axial/paraspinal and proximal weakness, elevated CK, muscle biopsy protein aggregates, and cardiac conduction abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Family history suggestive of inherited disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Cerebellar ataxia
Sensorineural high-frequency hearing loss
Elevated thyroid autoantibodies
Elevated rheumatoid factor and mildly positive ANA

data.diagnosis: Myofibrillar myopathy due to MYOT mutation (myotilinopathy)
data.description: An autosomal-dominant myofibrillar myopathy caused by MYOT mutations. It usually begins in adulthood with slowly progressive distal, proximal, or axial muscle weakness, elevated CK, and protein aggregates on muscle biopsy; some affected families have bent-spine syndrome.
symptoms_in_common: Gait difficulty and need for a walking stick
Pedigree consistent with possible autosomal-dominant inheritance
symptoms_not_in_common: Cerebellar ataxia without limb ataxia
Mild cognitive impairment
Sensorineural hearing loss
Frequent premature cardiac contractions
Autoimmune thyroid antibodies

data.diagnosis: Myofibrillar myopathy due to LDB3/ZASP mutation (ZASP-related myopathy)
data.description: A late-onset inherited myofibrillar myopathy caused by LDB3/ZASP variants, characterized by progressive muscle weakness, axial involvement or camptocormia, CK elevation, and sometimes cardiac arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy.
symptoms_in_common: Proximal leg weakness and stair-climbing difficulty
symptoms_not_in_common: Cerebellar ataxia
Sensorineural hearing loss
Mild cognitive impairment
Antithyroglobulin and antithyroid peroxidase antibody elevation
Elevated rheumatoid factor and ANA

data.diagnosis: Mitochondrial myopathy with ataxia and sensorineural hearing loss
data.description: Mitochondrial disorders can cause a combination of myopathy, exercise intolerance or weakness, cerebellar dysfunction, sensorineural hearing loss, cognitive changes, and cardiac rhythm abnormalities. The phenotype may be caused by mitochondrial DNA or nuclear-gene defects.
symptoms_not_in_common: Predominant severe paraspinal muscle atrophy with bent-spine syndrome
Normal lactate
Strong apparent autosomal-dominant family pattern of bent spine
Autoimmune thyroid antibodies
Elevated rheumatoid factor and ANA

data.description: A 2-year-old Korean male was admitted for evaluation and management of left hip pain. Physical examination revealed several palpable lymph nodes in the left inguinal area and an ill-defined heterogeneous mass-like lesion in the left anteromedial muscle. Peripheral blood examination showed hemoglobin 9.6 g/dL, white blood cell count 6.83 × 10^9/L, platelet count 182 × 10^9/L, and 5 atypical lymphocytes per 100 white blood cells. Immunophenotyping of neoplastic cells showed positivity for CD45 (99.0%), CD19 (94.84%), CD10 (27.64%), CD20 (94.24%), HLA-DR (95.70%), surface IgG lambda (96.45%), CD13 (22.46%), and CD117 (22.22%), and negativity for CD34 (0.01%), Tdt (0.64%), myeloperoxidase (0.01%), and various T-cell and myeloid markers.

An aggressive mature B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma that may involve lymph nodes, extranodal soft tissue, bone marrow, and peripheral blood. It typically shows a mature clonal B-cell phenotype with surface immunoglobulin expression and often CD10 positivity.
symptoms_in_common: Young child with rapidly concerning musculoskeletal/hip pain
Extranodal mass-like lesion in an anteromedial muscle
Mature B-cell immunophenotype with strong CD45, CD19, CD20, HLA-DR, and surface IgG lambda expression
Absence of TdT and CD34, supporting mature rather than precursor B cells
symptoms_not_in_common: CD13 and CD117 expression, which are aberrant and not typical of classic Burkitt lymphoma/leukemia
No reported abdominal mass, jaw mass, fever, weight loss, or night sweats

data.description: A mature aggressive B-cell lymphoma composed of large transformed B cells. It can present with nodal or extranodal masses but is substantially less common than Burkitt lymphoma in very young children.
symptoms_in_common: Hip pain related to a nearby mass lesion
Strong mature B-cell marker expression including CD19, CD20, CD45, HLA-DR, and surface immunoglobulin lambda restriction
symptoms_not_in_common: Age of 2 years is unusually young for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
CD10 expression can occur but is not universal
Peripheral blood atypical lymphocytes are less typical at presentation
CD13 and CD117 positivity are unusual
No reported constitutional B symptoms

data.description: A malignancy of immature B-cell precursors that commonly presents in children with marrow involvement, anemia, lymphadenopathy, bone pain, or soft-tissue masses. Typical cells express precursor markers such as TdT and often CD34.
symptoms_in_common: Age in the common pediatric range
Hip pain that could reflect marrow or soft-tissue involvement
Expression of B-cell markers CD19 and CD10
symptoms_not_in_common: Strong surface IgG lambda expression indicates mature clonal B cells rather than lymphoblasts
Strong CD20 expression is more consistent with mature B-cell lymphoma
TdT is negative
CD34 is negative
CD117 and CD13 expression are atypical for B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma

data.diagnosis: High-grade B-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified
data.description: An aggressive mature B-cell lymphoma with clinical and immunophenotypic features overlapping Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. It may present with extranodal disease, nodal enlargement, marrow involvement, and circulating lymphoma cells.
symptoms_in_common: Mature B-cell phenotype with CD19, CD20, CD45, HLA-DR, CD10, and surface immunoglobulin lambda expression
symptoms_not_in_common: This diagnostic category is uncommon in a 2-year-old child
CD13 and CD117 positivity are unusual aberrancies
No documented large-cell morphology, MYC/BCL2/BCL6 genetic findings, or other defining high-grade B-cell lymphoma features

diagnoses.name: B-cell lymphoma, unclassifiable, with features intermediate between diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and Burkitt lymphoma
diagnoses.title: B-cell lymphoma unclassifiable with features intermediate between Burkitt lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

data.description: A 12-year-old Malagasy boy consulted for a fever that had been evolving for two months, with a notion of trauma and pain in the right upper quadrant as well as chronic diarrhoea. A parasitological examination of the stool found eggs of Schistosoma mansoni. An ultrasound and a CT scan were then ordered.

data.diagnosis: Hepatosplenic schistosomiasis due to Schistosoma mansoni
data.description: Chronic S. mansoni infection can cause intestinal disease and egg-induced periportal hepatic fibrosis (Symmers pipestem fibrosis), leading to hepatosplenomegaly and portal hypertension while liver function may initially remain preserved.
symptoms_in_common: Stool examination positive for Schistosoma mansoni eggs
Imaging appearance compatible with hepatosplenic involvement and periportal fibrosis
symptoms_not_in_common: History of trauma is not a typical cause or feature of schistosomiasis

data.description: Intestinal infection with S. mansoni results from deposition of parasite eggs in the bowel wall, producing chronic inflammation, abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea, and sometimes blood loss or colonic polyps.
symptoms_in_common: Schistosoma mansoni eggs detected in stool
symptoms_not_in_common: Right upper-quadrant pain is less typical unless there is associated hepatic disease
The apparent hepatic imaging abnormalities are not explained by isolated intestinal schistosomiasis
History of trauma is not typical

data.description: A pyogenic liver abscess is a bacterial collection within the liver that commonly causes persistent fever, right upper-quadrant pain, and focal hepatic abnormalities on ultrasound or CT.
symptoms_in_common: Possible focal liver abnormality on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: Chronic diarrhoea is not a defining feature
Schistosoma mansoni eggs in stool do not establish a pyogenic abscess
Diffuse periportal/hepatosplenic changes would be less typical than a discrete fluid-containing abscess
History of trauma is not usually associated

data.diagnosis: Traumatic hepatic hematoma or liver contusion
data.description: Blunt abdominal trauma can produce liver contusion or hematoma, presenting with right upper-quadrant pain and a focal hepatic lesion on imaging.
symptoms_not_in_common: Two months of persistent fever is atypical unless the hematoma becomes infected
Chronic diarrhoea is not typical
Schistosoma mansoni eggs in stool are unrelated to traumatic liver injury
Diffuse hepatosplenic/periportal abnormalities are not typical of an isolated traumatic hematoma

data.description: A 44-year-old man presented with severe substernal burning chest pain radiating to the left arm დაწყening him from sleep 1 hour prior, with nausea and nonbloody vomiting. He had had similar less intense intermittent chest pain for 1 month, lasting hours to days and temporarily relieved by antacids and omeprazole. He denied dyspnea, fever, cough, trauma, edema, immobility, tobacco, alcohol, or illicit drug use; no family history of premature coronary artery disease. His history was otherwise unremarkable, though he recalled thrombocytosis (~600,000/mm³) 12 years earlier and reported intermittent generalized pruritus after hot showers, without bleeding, thrombosis, or neurologic symptoms. On exam, he was afebrile, in marked distress clutching his chest, with normal heart rhythm, no JVD or leg edema, normal lung exam, and a nontender chest and abdomen. Labs showed troponin 0.08 ng/mL, WBC 22,000/mm³ with neutrophilia and bandemia, platelets 771,000/mm³, hemoglobin 17.5 g/dL, and glucose 192 mg/dL.
Acute myocardial infarction caused by abrupt coronary artery occlusion, with ECG findings suggesting anterior/anterolateral myocardial injury, typically involving the left anterior descending artery.
symptoms_in_common: Radiation of pain to the left arm
Marked distress while clutching his chest
Anterior precordial ST-segment elevation on ECG
symptoms_not_in_common: Intermittent chest pain lasting hours to days for 1 month with temporary relief from antacids and omeprazole
Intermittent generalized pruritus after hot showers
Marked thrombocytosis

data.description: A JAK2-associated myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by increased red-cell mass and often elevated platelets and leukocytes; it can cause aquagenic pruritus and arterial thrombosis, including coronary thrombosis.
symptoms_in_common: Intermittent generalized pruritus after hot showers
Possible arterial thrombotic complication presenting as myocardial infarction
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe acute substernal chest pain with left-arm radiation is not a primary manifestation unless caused by thrombosis
Nausea and vomiting are not typical baseline manifestations
No reported headache, visual disturbances, dizziness, erythromelalgia, or splenomegaly

data.description: A chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm causing persistent platelet elevation and increased risk of arterial or venous thrombosis; some patients have microvascular symptoms or bleeding.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent/recurrent thrombocytosis, including a prior platelet count around 600,000/mm³
Possible coronary arterial thrombosis causing acute myocardial infarction
Leukocytosis can occur in this disorder
symptoms_not_in_common: Aquagenic pruritus is more characteristic of polycythemia vera
Elevated hemoglobin is less typical if essential thrombocythemia is isolated
No history of erythromelalgia, headaches, visual symptoms, abnormal bleeding, or splenomegaly
Nausea and vomiting are not typical manifestations unless secondary to myocardial infarction

data.diagnosis: Acute coronary syndrome due to coronary thrombosis associated with a myeloproliferative neoplasm
data.description: Acute coronary ischemia may occur when hypercoagulability from a myeloproliferative neoplasm, such as polycythemia vera or essential thrombocythemia, causes in-situ coronary thrombosis despite few traditional atherosclerotic risk factors.
symptoms_in_common: Acute severe substernal chest pain radiating to the left arm
Lack of conventional coronary artery disease risk factors
History suggestive of a chronic myeloproliferative disorder

data.description: Newborn girl admitted to the NICU after cardiorespiratory arrest at delivery. Pregnancy was complicated by maternal hepatitis C infection, treated urogenital Chlamydia trachomatis infection in the second trimester, gestational hypertension, and serial prenatal ultrasounds showing right-sided urinary tract dilatation from 20 weeks to term. At 40 weeks, after prolonged labor and cesarean delivery for nonreassuring fetal status with meconium-stained fluid and breech presentation, the infant was born limp with no respiratory effort. She required 16 minutes of resuscitation with intubation, CPR, epinephrine, and saline boluses before return of spontaneous circulation. Apgar scores were 1, 0, 0, 1, and 3 at 1, 5, 10, 15, and 20 minutes. On NICU admission, she was hypothermic (34.9°C) with heart rate 141 bpm and blood pressure 84/59 mm Hg; therapeutic hypothermia was started.

data.description: 54-year-old man with history of polysubstance abuse and treatment-naïve hepatitis C presented with altered mental status. He was afebrile, drowsy, and hypertensive (172/110 mmHg) with distended jugular veins and bibasilar crackles. Labs showed severe renal dysfunction (creatinine 16.0 mg/dL, BUN 99 mg/dL), mild anemia (hemoglobin 11.3 g/dL), proteinuria, elevated LDH, rare schistocytes, and reduced C3 with normal C4; C3 hypocomplementemia persisted during hospitalization. Urine toxicology was positive for cocaine and metabolites. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Renal ultrasound showed echogenic kidneys measuring 9.8 cm and 10.3 cm. Family history included a sister with renal failure of unclear cause requiring dialysis at age 45.

data.description: 44-year-old Chinese woman, previously healthy, with 7 weeks of progressively worsening nausea and vomiting and 13 kg weight loss. No abdominal pain, distension, or diarrhea. Symptoms did not improve with 3 weeks of antidepressants, prokinetics, and anti-emetics. Eight days after admission, she developed metabolic alkalosis, acute respiratory failure, and neurological deficits. Examination showed right-sided limb paralysis, horizontal nystagmus, loss of pharyngeal reflex, reduced tendon reflexes on the right, and bilateral Babinski sign. Laboratory studies were unremarkable, including normal liver, kidney, thyroid, autoimmune, and glucose tests; serum AQP4-IgG was negative, but cerebrospinal fluid AQP4-IgG was positive. Prior gastroscopy and abdominal CT were normal.

data.description: 51-year-old man undergoing venesection for haemochromatosis. During procedure, experienced sudden gurgling sensation up his arm, followed by severe central crushing chest pain with radiation to jaw and left arm, severe dyspnoea, and left sided hemiparesis and dysphasia. On arrival to hospital: hypoxic (oxygen saturation 88% on room air), left hemiplegia (resolved within 15 minutes). Initial ECG showed T-wave inversion inferiorly. Troponin I was raised at 0.14 μg/L (ref 0-0.08 μg/L). Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study showed right-to-left shunting during normal respiration and Valsalva. Baseline right heart pressures were normal. Transoesophageal echocardiogram confirmed patent foramen ovale with passage of bubbles.

data.diagnosis: Venous air embolism with paradoxical systemic air embolism through a patent foramen ovale

Severe central crushing chest pain radiating to the jaw and left arm

Documented right-to-left shunt through a patent foramen ovale

data.description: 32-year-old man with a 10-week history of violaceous skin rash followed 1 week later by progressive generalized muscle pain and weakness, with difficulty walking, rising from a squat, and climbing stairs. Rash involved the eyelids, elbows, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, knees, and later the extensor surfaces of the fingers, elbows, and knees. Prior exam showed heliotrope rash, periungual edema, erythematous fingertip papules, and moderate-to-severe bilateral weakness of the deltoids, triceps, hip flexors, hamstrings, and quadriceps, with normal muscle bulk, tone, reflexes, and sensation. On admission, he had bilateral heliotrope rash, nontender periungual erythema, pitting edema of the arms and legs, diminished breath sounds at both lung bases, hypoactive bowel sounds, and severe proximal weakness with inability to lift arms, legs, or head against gravity. Past history included meniscal repair 10 years earlier; he did not smoke or use illicit drugs.
An idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by symmetric proximal muscle weakness and distinctive cutaneous findings, including heliotrope rash and Gottron papules/sign.

data.description: A previously healthy 50-year-old man presented with acute-onset dysarthria and was found to be febrile with respiratory distress and lethargy. The apex beat was located in the sixth intercostal space, 1.5 cm outside the midclavicular line. Cardiac auscultation revealed a grade 4/6 systolic murmur that was most prominent at the apex. The leukocyte count was 10,620/mm³ with neutrophils at 10,350/mm³, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 68 mm/h. Blood culture was positive for group A β-hemolytic streptococcus. data.description: A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 12-hour history of hematuria. data.description: 27-year-old female, 162cm tall, 30kg weight. Born after normal pregnancy/delivery. No family history of neurological diseases. Normal early development. At age 8, muscle biopsy showed mitochondrial myopathy of pleoconial type. At age 24, had sudden syncope. At age 26, had stroke with general weakness, aphagia, and dysarthria. Lab findings: plasma lactate 21.8 mg/dL (elevated), normal CBC/electrolytes/BUN/creatinine, free T4 1.76 ng/dL, TSH 0.04 μIU/mL, C3 13 mg/dL (low), C4 18 mg/dL (normal). symptoms_not_in_common: Disease onset at age 53 is atypical because Darier disease usually begins in adolescence

No classic widespread greasy keratotic papules in seborrheic areas were described
No nail abnormalities such as V-shaped nicking or longitudinal red-white streaks
No oral mucosal cobblestoning was present

data.description: A rare flexural variant of pemphigus vulgaris in which painful flaccid blisters evolve into vegetating, eroded, malodorous plaques, often involving the axillae and groin.

Vegetative or thickened appearance of flexural plaques

No oral or other mucosal involvement
No reported widespread flaccid bullae
Summer-related worsening and chronic localized flexural disease are more typical of Hailey-Hailey disease

data.description: A velvety hyperpigmented thickening of flexural skin, often associated with obesity and insulin resistance; friction, moisture, and secondary infection can cause intertrigo with odor and maceration.
symptoms_in_common: Possible familial metabolic risk, given a sibling with diabetes
Maceration and malodor may occur with secondary intertrigo

Painful erosions and recurrent crusted lesions are not typical of uncomplicated acanthosis nigricans
Hypopigmented areas are not characteristic
Acantholysis on biopsy would not be expected
A similar chronic blistering rash in a sibling is not explained by acanthosis nigricans alone

data.description: A yeast infection of moist skin folds causing erythema, maceration, fissuring, soreness, and sometimes malodor; obesity and warm weather increase risk.
