Blistering is uncommon
Irregular hyperpigmentation and hypopigmentation with marked thickening are not classic
Multiple skin tags are not caused by candidiasis
Histologic acantholysis would not be expected
No satellite pustules or papules were described

data.description: A 22-year-old female presented with a gradually increasing pelvic mass with tenderness for 1 month. There was no evidence of previous trauma or fever, and no history of other medical or surgical disease and no evidence of pregnancy. On physical examination, there was a palpable mass with tenderness in her left pelvic area.

A benign, localized heterotopic bone-forming lesion within soft tissue or muscle, often developing after trauma but sometimes occurring without a recognized injury. Imaging commonly shows peripheral, zonal calcification/ossification without destruction of adjacent bone.
symptoms_in_common: Peripheral calcified or ossified appearance on imaging with no clear destructive pelvic bone lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: No history of preceding trauma, although many cases can be nontraumatic
Relatively short 1-month history for a lesion with prominent mineralization

data.description: A rare malignant mesenchymal tumor that produces osteoid or bone in soft tissue without direct origin from bone. It may appear as a painful enlarging mineralized soft-tissue mass.

symptoms_not_in_common: Age 22 years is much younger than the usual older-adult presentation
Only 1 month of symptoms
No constitutional symptoms, although these are not required

data.description: A malignant cartilage-producing tumor arising in soft tissues, sometimes in the pelvis or proximal limbs. It can form a slowly enlarging painful mass with stippled, ring-and-arc, or peripheral calcifications.

Rapidly apparent course over only 1 month
No reported long-standing mass or chronic symptoms

Prominent mineralization would usually imply a longer duration than 1 month

data.description: A common benign ovarian germ-cell tumor in young women that may contain fat, calcification, teeth, or bone. It can present as a palpable pelvic mass with pain or tenderness, especially if large or complicated by torsion.
symptoms_in_common: Calcified components may be present on radiographs and CT

No reported ovarian/adnexal origin

No reported fat-containing component

data.description: 36-year-old female with no past medical history developed progressive lower-limb and paraspinal muscle spasms over 3 months, worsening over 6 months to wheelchair dependence. She later required regular IVIG (90 g every 12 days), diazepam 30 mg/day, and morphine up to 60 mg/day for pain. On examination, she had brisk reflexes and severe clonus, with spasms severe enough to impair breathing and requiring intermittent oxygen.

A rare autoimmune neurologic disorder characterized by progressive axial and proximal limb rigidity, painful stimulus-sensitive muscle spasms, and hyperexcitability of motor pathways; often associated with anti-GAD65 antibodies and may respond to IVIG and benzodiazepines.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive paraspinal and lower-limb muscle stiffness/spasms
Progressive functional disability leading to wheelchair dependence
Spasms involving axial muscles and impairing breathing
Electrophysiologic findings consistent with continuous motor-unit activity and exaggerated reflex responses
symptoms_not_in_common: No symptoms clearly atypical for SPS are described

symptoms_in_common: Rapidly progressive severe rigidity and spasms
Potential response to IVIG and diazepam
Marked motor hyperexcitability on electrophysiologic testing

symptoms_in_common: Severe painful axial and limb spasms
Spasms severe enough to interfere with breathing
Electrophysiologic evidence of excessive motor activity
symptoms_not_in_common: Antibody status is not provided

Bulbar symptoms and autonomic dysfunction are not reported

symptoms_not_in_common: The course progressed over months rather than the usual acute to subacute onset

Long-term IVIG-responsive disease is not typical for tetanus

data.description: 46-year-old woman presented with frequent collapse. Medical history included carotid endarterectomy in 2005 following a small right hemispheric stroke, and hypercholesterolaemia. No previous dermatological or scalp problems. Current medications: clopidogrel 75mg, aspirin 80mg, and simvastatin 40mg daily.

A chronic large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, often causing carotid or subclavian stenosis/occlusion in younger women. Reduced cerebral and scalp perfusion can cause syncope, stroke, and ischemic scalp ulceration.
symptoms_in_common: Frequent collapse, compatible with cerebral hypoperfusion
Previous ischemic stroke at an unusually young age
History of carotid endarterectomy, suggesting significant carotid arterial disease
Scalp ischemia/ulceration shown in the image
Angiographic appearance of major neck-vessel stenosis or occlusive disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No constitutional inflammatory symptoms such as fever, fatigue, weight loss, or limb claudication were reported

data.diagnosis: Severe atherosclerotic carotid and great-vessel occlusive disease
data.description: Progressive narrowing or occlusion of the carotid, brachiocephalic, or subclavian arteries due to atherosclerosis. Severe disease may impair cerebral and external carotid circulation, causing collapse, stroke, and scalp ischemia.
symptoms_in_common: Scalp ulcer/necrosis compatible with poor external carotid circulation
Neck-vessel stenotic/occlusive changes on angiographic imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: The severity of carotid disease at a relatively young age is less typical for uncomplicated atherosclerosis

data.diagnosis: Giant cell arteritis with scalp ischemia/necrosis
data.description: A granulomatous vasculitis of medium and large arteries, especially temporal and extracranial carotid branches. Severe inflammation can cause scalp tenderness, ulceration, or necrosis and may lead to ischemic neurologic complications.
symptoms_in_common: Possible vascular insufficiency involving branches of the carotid circulation
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 46 years is younger than typical, as giant cell arteritis usually occurs after age 50
No new headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, or systemic inflammatory symptoms were reported
Frequent collapse is not a classic presenting symptom

data.diagnosis: Subclavian steal syndrome or brachiocephalic artery stenosis
data.description: Stenosis of the proximal subclavian or brachiocephalic artery can divert blood away from cerebral circulation through collateral pathways, causing vertebrobasilar insufficiency and episodes of presyncope or syncope.
symptoms_in_common: Frequent collapse consistent with transient cerebral hypoperfusion
Angiographic evidence suggestive of proximal great-vessel stenosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Scalp ulceration/necrosis is not typical of isolated subclavian steal syndrome
No arm claudication, arm weakness, or exertional arm symptoms were reported

data.description: 60-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate and adalimumab. Four months before admission, she developed pain and stiffness in the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, right ankle, and both knees. Six weeks before admission, she had severe arthralgia, low-grade fever, livedo reticularis on the legs, and purpuric lesions around the malleoli, with anemia, leukopenia, neutropenia, hypergammaglobulinemia, ANA 1:640, low C4, positive rheumatoid factor, and positive cryoglobulins. On admission after a burn from an electric heater, she had fever and pancytopenia without hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy. Blood, urine, and sputum cultures, imaging, CMV PCR, and tuberculin testing were negative. She had traveled to Athens seven months earlier and stayed with relatives who kept several dogs.

A systemic protozoal infection transmitted by sandflies, endemic in the Mediterranean region. It is more severe in patients receiving immunosuppressive therapy, including anti-TNF agents. The smear image is consistent with intracellular Leishmania amastigotes.
symptoms_in_common: Pancytopenia including anemia, leukopenia, and neutropenia
Travel to Athens, a Mediterranean endemic area
Exposure to dogs, important reservoir hosts for Leishmania infantum
Negative routine bacterial cultures and viral testing
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of hepatosplenomegaly
Absence of lymphadenopathy
Livedo reticularis
Purpuric lesions around the malleoli
High-titer ANA with low C4

data.description: An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis caused by circulating cryoglobulins, often associated with autoimmune disease, chronic infection, or lymphoproliferative disorders.
symptoms_in_common: Palpable purpuric lesions around the malleoli
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe pancytopenia
Neutropenia
Travel to an area endemic for visceral leishmaniasis
Dog exposure
Intracellular organisms compatible with amastigotes on smear

data.diagnosis: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) or lupus-like autoimmune syndrome
data.description: A systemic autoimmune disease characterized by autoantibody production, immune-complex formation, hypocomplementemia, cytopenias, arthritis, and cutaneous vascular manifestations. Anti-TNF therapy can rarely induce a lupus-like syndrome.
symptoms_not_in_common: Positive cryoglobulins as a central feature
Marked neutropenia with systemic infectious presentation
Travel-associated dog exposure suggesting zoonotic infection
Intracellular amastigote-like organisms on smear
Positive rheumatoid factor alone is not specific for SLE

data.description: A complication of long-standing seropositive rheumatoid arthritis characterized by neutropenia, usually with splenomegaly and increased susceptibility to infection.
symptoms_not_in_common: No splenomegaly
Pancytopenia rather than predominantly neutropenia
Hypergammaglobulinemia with positive cryoglobulins
Low C4
Livedo reticularis and purpuric lesions
Travel and dog exposure suggesting visceral leishmaniasis
Intracellular amastigote-like organisms on smear

data.description: A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome that can be triggered by infections, malignancy, or autoimmune disease and may cause persistent fever and severe cytopenias. Visceral leishmaniasis is a recognized trigger.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported hepatosplenomegaly
No reported markedly elevated ferritin, triglycerides, or liver dysfunction
No documented hemophagocytosis
Livedo reticularis and cryoglobulinemic purpura are not typical primary HLH manifestations
The smear findings favor direct Leishmania infection rather than HLH alone

data.description: A 25-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the emergency department for evaluation of a hyperpigmented lesion on the shin. The lesion appeared as a small reddish-brown macule 3 years ago and has gradually increased in size. During the past several months, the lesion has become indented and increasingly tender. The patient denies systemic symptoms, including fevers and chills, and is primarily concerned about the changing appearance of the lesion and the new-onset tenderness. Laboratory evaluation shows a random blood glucose level of 217 mg/dL (12 mmol/L).

A chronic granulomatous skin disorder strongly associated with diabetes mellitus, characterized by slowly enlarging yellow-brown to reddish plaques on the shins with central atrophy, telangiectasia, and possible tenderness or ulceration. Histology typically shows necrobiotic collagen with palisading granulomatous inflammation.
symptoms_in_common: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with elevated random glucose
Tenderness developing in a chronic lesion

data.description: A benign inflammatory dermatosis consisting of dermal palisading granulomas, often presenting as annular papules or plaques on the extremities. Generalized forms may be associated with diabetes, but lesions are usually asymptomatic and lack the characteristic atrophic yellow center of necrobiosis lipoidica.
symptoms_not_in_common: Pretibial lesion with central indentation/atrophy
Yellow-brown central appearance
Increasing tenderness
Long-standing plaque with changes characteristic of necrobiosis

data.description: A common diabetic microvascular skin finding causing small, round or oval, brown, atrophic macules on the shins, often called shin spots. They are typically multiple, asymptomatic, and do not progressively enlarge into inflammatory plaques.
symptoms_not_in_common: Single lesion gradually enlarging over 3 years
Prominent reddish inflammatory border
Yellow-brown plaque-like appearance
New-onset tenderness
Histologic granulomatous/necrobiotic pattern

data.description: Localized dermal accumulation of glycosaminoglycans, most often associated with Graves disease, causing nonpitting thickened plaques or nodules on the shins with an orange-peel texture. It is not typically associated with diabetes alone.
symptoms_not_in_common: Known diabetes rather than thyroid disease
Initially small macule that progressively enlarged
Central atrophy/indentation rather than skin thickening
Yellow-brown necrobiotic appearance
Tenderness is not typical
No reported Graves disease symptoms

data.description: 14-year-old boy with 2 days of acute fear of choking while swallowing after choking on chicken at dinner, followed by fear of eating, vomiting with attempts to eat, and markedly reduced oral intake and fluids. He had several weeks of inspiratory stridor during sleep. On presentation he was anxious, with drooling, persistent involuntary burping, and dry oral mucosa; later exam showed hypertonic leg muscles and a mildly positive left Chvostek sign. Past history included infantile gastroesophageal reflux, milk-protein allergy, sensory-integration training, keratosis pilaris, and eczema. He was born at term after nuchal cord with low initial Apgar scores and needed resuscitation. Labs showed severe hypocalcemia with hyperphosphatemia, elevated parathyroid hormone, and mildly elevated TSH with normal free thyroxine.

A disorder of resistance to parathyroid hormone, usually caused by abnormal methylation at the GNAS locus. It produces hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and elevated parathyroid hormone despite adequate hormone production.
symptoms_in_common: Difficulty swallowing and fear of choking potentially related to hypocalcemic neuromuscular irritability
symptoms_not_in_common: Several weeks of inspiratory stridor during sleep
Drooling
Persistent involuntary burping
History of eczema, keratosis pilaris, and milk-protein allergy
Acute onset after a witnessed choking episode

data.diagnosis: Hypocalcemic tetany due to parathyroid hormone resistance
data.description: Neuromuscular hyperexcitability caused by severe low serum calcium. In this case, the biochemical pattern suggests that the hypocalcemia is caused by resistance to parathyroid hormone.
symptoms_in_common: Possible laryngeal muscle irritability contributing to stridor
symptoms_not_in_common: Hyperphosphatemia and elevated parathyroid hormone are not features of tetany itself but identify the underlying cause
Persistent involuntary burping
History of infantile reflux
Eczema and keratosis pilaris
Milk-protein allergy

symptoms_in_common: Mildly elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone with normal free thyroxine
Neuromuscular irritability with hypertonia and positive Chvostek sign
symptoms_not_in_common: The reported methylation abnormality is more characteristic of PHP1B than PHP1A
No reported short stature
No reported round face
No reported brachydactyly
No reported obesity or subcutaneous ossifications
Sleep-related inspiratory stridor
Persistent burping and drooling

data.diagnosis: Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder (ARFID) triggered by choking fear

Markedly reduced food and fluid intake

Hyperphosphatemia
Elevated parathyroid hormone
Positive Chvostek sign
Hypertonic leg muscles
Abnormal GNAS methylation

data.description: 57-year-old woman with resected stage IIIC cutaneous melanoma presented with recurrent fever. Four months before admission, she developed bleeding from a right scalp lesion; evaluation showed ulcerated melanoma with positive margins. Three months before admission, she underwent wide local excision and neck lymph-node dissection, which revealed metastatic melanoma in 2 of 26 lymph nodes. Molecular testing showed BRAF V600E mutation. One month before admission, she started adjuvant dabrafenib and trametinib; fever and nausea developed the next day, improved after temporary discontinuation and antipyretics, then fever recurred two weeks before admission. On presentation, she was diaphoretic and ill-appearing, with temperature 40.2°C, pulse 108 beats per minute, oxygen saturation 94% on room air, and mild right upper-quadrant tenderness; no rash was present.

Systemic infection with Histoplasma capsulatum, often involving lungs, liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and bone marrow; tissue may show granulomatous inflammation containing small intracellular yeasts highlighted by fungal stains.
symptoms_in_common: Mild right upper-quadrant tenderness suggesting hepatic involvement
Hepatic and splenic lesions on imaging
Granulomatous inflammation with fungal organisms on tissue staining
symptoms_not_in_common: Very close onset of the first fever episode after starting dabrafenib and trametinib
No reported cough, dyspnea, or weight loss

data.description: Pyrexia is a common adverse effect of combined BRAF and MEK inhibitor therapy, particularly dabrafenib plus trametinib. Fever may be recurrent, high grade, and associated with nausea, rigors, dehydration, and tachycardia.

Improvement after temporary discontinuation and antipyretics
symptoms_not_in_common: Right upper-quadrant tenderness
Pulmonary lesions or nodules on imaging
Hepatic and splenic lesions on imaging
Granulomatous tissue inflammation with fungal organisms

Nausea as a prominent early symptom
Fungal organisms demonstrated by fungal staining rather than acid-fast bacilli
No reported chronic cough, weight loss, or night sweats before the acute illness

data.diagnosis: Sarcoidosis or sarcoid-like reaction related to BRAF/MEK inhibitor therapy
data.description: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disorder that may affect lungs, lymph nodes, liver, and spleen. BRAF/MEK inhibitors can rarely trigger sarcoid-like granulomatous reactions.
symptoms_not_in_common: High fever to 40.2°C
Marked diaphoresis and acutely ill appearance
Nausea
Fungal organisms on tissue staining
No reported hilar lymphadenopathy, skin lesions, uveitis, or chronic respiratory symptoms

data.description: Melanoma can recur after surgery and spread to lymph nodes, lungs, liver, spleen, bone, brain, and other organs. Advanced disease may produce constitutional symptoms and abdominal discomfort from liver involvement.

Hepatic and splenic lesions on imaging

data.description: 59-year-old man with history of prostate cancer metastatic to lumbar spine and periaortic lymph nodes diagnosed in 2001, with initial PSA of 11.3 ng/mL. Later returned with right upper quadrant abdominal pain, tachycardia but afebrile. Physical exam showed positive Murphy's sign and palpable gallbladder. Afebrile presentation

Pain specifically localized to the right upper quadrant rather than typical epigastric pain

Initial markedly elevated lipase, which is more suggestive of pancreatitis
Normal bilirubin
Known metastatic prostate cancer, which raises concern for malignant obstruction rather than routine gallstone disease

data.description: 13-year-old Caucasian boy with a history of Addison’s disease, dysphagia, muscle weakness, excessive fatigue, and recent gait ataxia. Born at term with bilateral cryptorchidism, inguinal hernia, and hypospadias. Development was initially normal but later showed global delay and mild intellectual disability by age 9. He had absent tear production since infancy. At age 2, he developed recurrent vomiting, failure to thrive, and progressive skin pigmentation; at age 4, recurrent hypotonia, hypoglycemia, and hypothermia led to diagnosis of Addison’s disease. Severe progressive dysphagia began at age 11, requiring liquids to swallow. Examination showed severe hyperpigmentation and hyperkeratosis of the elbows and knuckles, facial dysmorphism, dysarthria, nasal speech, saccadic eye movements with horizontal gaze nystagmus, dilated pupils with poor light response, mild bilateral optic atrophy, distal arm weakness and wasting, milder leg weakness, unsteady gait, hyperreflexia, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Labs showed markedly elevated ACTH with normal electrolytes, aldosterone, and renin; very long chain fatty acids were normal.

Hyperreflexia and bilateral extensor plantar responses

Developmental delay and mild intellectual disability

Hypospadias
Inguinal hernia
Facial dysmorphism
Marked hyperkeratosis of elbows and knuckles

Vomiting, hypoglycemia, and hypothermia due to adrenal insufficiency

data.description: 55-year-old woman with a 13-year history of invasive ductal carcinoma of the right breast and stage IV metastatic disease to bone, lungs, and liver, status post mastectomy, multiple systemic therapies, and stem-cell transplantation 8 years earlier. Most recent treatment was anastrozole for 3 months with paracetamol for pain. She developed progressive generalized weakness and episodic confusion over several days, rapidly worsening to unresponsiveness. On admission, she was found on the floor, disoriented, with lower leg weakness and inability to follow basic instructions. Examination showed she was awake but unresponsive and uncooperative, without initial focal neurologic deficits. Vital signs were notable for mild tachycardia without fever; blood pressure was normal. Baseline brain MRI 2 weeks earlier was normal.

data.diagnosis: Cerebral fat embolism syndrome related to bone marrow necrosis from metastatic breast cancer

In metastatic cancer, marrow infiltration or bone marrow necrosis can release marrow fat even without trauma.
symptoms_in_common: Multifocal bilateral brain lesions with diffusion restriction
MRI evidence of punctate hemorrhagic lesions/microhemorrhages
Extensive bone metastatic disease, which can predispose to marrow necrosis and fat embolization
No focal neurologic deficit initially despite severe altered mental status

No preceding traumatic long-bone fracture or orthopedic procedure

Acute to subacute confusion and reduced responsiveness
Multiple bilateral diffusion-restricted brain lesions consistent with acute ischemic injury
Possible small hemorrhagic components within ischemic lesions

The diffuse encephalopathy is more prominent than typical territorial embolic stroke symptoms

data.diagnosis: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis with cerebral emboli
data.description: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis involves sterile platelet-fibrin vegetations on cardiac valves, most often in patients with advanced malignancy. Embolization can cause multiple acute ischemic strokes in different cerebral territories.
symptoms_in_common: Metastatic malignancy, a major risk factor for sterile valvular vegetations
Multifocal bilateral diffusion-restricted lesions suggesting embolic cerebral infarctions
No fever, which is compatible with noninfectious endocarditis
symptoms_not_in_common: No cardiac murmur or known valve vegetation reported
No systemic embolic manifestations described
Microhemorrhagic MRI pattern may be less typical than in cerebral fat embolism

data.diagnosis: Cerebral thrombotic microangiopathy associated with malignancy
data.description: Cancer-associated thrombotic microangiopathy can produce widespread small-vessel thrombosis, ischemic brain injury, encephalopathy, and occasionally hemorrhagic lesions. It may occur in advanced metastatic cancer or with certain cancer therapies.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple small bilateral ischemic-appearing lesions on MRI
Punctate hemorrhagic abnormalities on susceptibility imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No anemia, thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, renal dysfunction, or hemolysis reported
Blood pressure was normal rather than markedly elevated
No fever or other systemic inflammatory findings reported

data.description: PRES is a neurotoxic syndrome characterized by vasogenic edema, usually involving posterior cerebral regions, causing altered mental status, seizures, headache, and visual symptoms. It may occur with cancer therapy, renal dysfunction, hypertension, or endothelial injury.
symptoms_in_common: Cancer treatment history and potential endothelial injury
Possible hemorrhagic foci can occur in PRES
symptoms_not_in_common: Blood pressure was normal rather than severely elevated
No seizures, headache, or visual symptoms reported
Prominent diffusion restriction suggesting multifocal infarction is less typical than vasogenic edema
The MRI pattern of numerous punctate lesions and microhemorrhages is more suggestive of embolic or fat-embolism phenomena

data.description: 54-year-old woman with no significant past medical history presented with 1 month of progressive weakness in all four extremities and sensory changes, followed by urinary difficulty. On examination, she had increased deep tendon reflexes, positive Babinski sign, bilateral Hoffman's and Tromner's signs, and decreased motor strength (MRC 2 on the right, MRC 4 on the left). Sensory loss included decreased pinprick and temperature below the C4 level, more on the left, and decreased vibration and proprioception, more on the right. Serologic autoimmune studies and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were normal; ACE was mildly elevated. Brain MRI, chest and abdominal CT, and nerve conduction study showed no other organ involvement.

A rare manifestation of sarcoidosis in which noncaseating granulomatous inflammation involves the spinal cord, producing an enhancing intramedullary cervical lesion and progressive myelopathy. Histology typically shows noncaseating granulomas with multinucleated giant cells and negative infectious stains.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute progressive weakness in all four extremities
Upper motor neuron signs including hyperreflexia, Babinski sign, Hoffman's sign, and Tromner's sign
Dissociated sensory loss involving pinprick/temperature and posterior-column modalities
Urinary difficulty due to spinal cord involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: No pulmonary, lymph-node, skin, ocular, or other systemic sarcoidosis involvement identified
Normal cerebrospinal fluid analysis

data.description: An acute or subacute inflammatory spinal cord syndrome causing motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction below a spinal cord lesion, sometimes without an identifiable autoimmune, infectious, or systemic cause.
symptoms_in_common: Hyperreflexia and pathological reflexes indicating myelopathy
Loss of pinprick, temperature, vibration, and proprioception
No clear systemic autoimmune disease or infection on initial testing
symptoms_not_in_common: Pathologic granulomatous inflammation with giant cells would not be typical
Mild ACE elevation is not typical
A focal persistently enhancing intramedullary lesion may be less typical than diffuse inflammatory cord signal change

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory demyelinating disorder, commonly associated with aquaporin-4 antibodies, that can cause severe myelitis and optic neuritis. Spinal lesions often extend across three or more vertebral segments.
symptoms_in_common: Quadriparesis with upper motor neuron signs
Potential longitudinal spinal cord lesion on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: No optic neuritis or other visual symptoms reported
Normal cerebrospinal fluid findings do not strongly support active NMOSD
Granulomatous pathology is not typical of NMOSD
Mild ACE elevation is not characteristic

data.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that may cause focal spinal cord lesions, sensory symptoms, weakness, spasticity, and bladder dysfunction.
symptoms_in_common: Upper motor neuron weakness and hyperreflexia
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 54 years is less typical for initial presentation
Rapidly progressive severe quadriparesis from a single cervical lesion is less typical
Brain MRI reportedly showed no other lesions
Normal cerebrospinal fluid analysis does not support typical multiple sclerosis findings
Noncaseating granulomatous pathology is not typical

data.diagnosis: Intramedullary spinal cord tumor (such as ependymoma or astrocytoma)
data.description: A primary tumor arising within the spinal cord that can produce progressive cervical myelopathy through cord expansion, tract dysfunction, and possible contrast enhancement.
symptoms_not_in_common: Granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells is not typical of ependymoma or astrocytoma
Mildly elevated ACE is not expected
The inflammatory histologic appearance favors sarcoidosis or another granulomatous disorder rather than neoplasm

data.description: 33-year-old male with 20 days of cough and small amounts of yellow-white sticky sputum after a cold, without hemoptysis, fever, chills, dyspnea, or initial chest pain. He was treated at a local clinic with IV therapy without improvement. Over the past 7 days, cough worsened, especially at night causing sleep disturbance, and was sometimes accompanied by right-sided chest pain. No significant past medical history. Smoked about 10 cigarettes/day for over 10 years; no alcohol use. Physical exam: T 36.2℃, P 112/min, R 19/min, BP 126/85 mmHg; symmetric chest, normal percussion, coarse breath sounds in both lungs, and a small amount of wet rales in the right lung.

A chronic, suppurative lung infection caused by Actinomyces species, often producing mass-like consolidation, cavitation, abscess formation, and pleuritic chest pain. It may mimic malignancy or tuberculosis and can fail to respond to nonspecific short-course antibiotic treatment.
symptoms_in_common: CT appearance of right lower-lobe consolidation with cavitary or necrotic change
Lack of improvement after initial intravenous treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No chills
No hemoptysis
Relatively short symptom duration for a typically chronic infection

data.description: A localized destructive bacterial infection of lung tissue that causes necrosis and cavitation, often with purulent sputum, focal crackles, and pleuritic chest pain. Aspiration-related anaerobic infection and Staphylococcus, Klebsiella, or other bacteria can cause this pattern.
symptoms_in_common: Wet rales in the right lung
Right lower-lobe consolidation and cavitary/necrotic appearance on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: No fever
No chills
No dyspnea
Only a small amount of sputum
No reported foul-smelling or large-volume purulent sputum

data.description: An inflammatory lung disorder in which granulation tissue plugs form in distal airways and alveoli, often after a respiratory infection. It can present as persistent cough with focal consolidation and may be mistaken for bacterial pneumonia or cancer.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent symptoms despite initial antibiotic-type intravenous therapy
Focal right lower-lobe consolidation on CT
Pathology appearance compatible with inflammatory and organizing alveolar injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Yellow-white sputum is less typical because cough is often dry
Cavitary or abscess-like CT change is less typical
Localized wet rales are less characteristic than diffuse or patchy findings
Right-sided chest pain is not a prominent typical feature

data.description: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection can cause persistent cough, sputum production, focal infiltrates, cavitation, and chest discomfort. Although classically upper-lobe predominant, lower-lobe disease may occur.
symptoms_in_common: Possible cavitary pulmonary lesion on CT
Failure to improve with routine nonspecific treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute onset after a cold
Only 20 days of symptoms
No fever
No night sweats
No weight loss
No hemoptysis
Predominantly right lower-lobe involvement rather than classic upper-lobe disease

data.diagnosis: Primary lung cancer with post-obstructive pneumonia
data.description: A bronchial tumor can obstruct an airway and lead to retained secretions, recurrent infection, focal consolidation, and cavitation. Smoking is a risk factor, although primary lung cancer is less common at age 33.
symptoms_in_common: Focal right lower-lobe abnormality on CT
Failure to improve after initial treatment
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age
Short 20-day illness duration
Symptoms beginning after a cold
No hemoptysis
No weight loss
No persistent dyspnea
Wet rales and purulent sputum more strongly suggest active infection

data.description: A 64-year-old male patient from Smoljanci, Istria presented with firm, migrating nodules in the brachial region without history of serious disease. He had no travel outside Croatia but spent recreational time in forests and islands near his residence and owned a pet dog. Physical examination revealed a painless, well-demarcated subcutaneous nodule in his right upper arm measuring 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.0 cm. Ultrasonographic findings of the nodule appeared normal. Laboratory tests showed total blood counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein within normal values. Serologic results for trichinosis, toxocariasis, schistosomiasis, distomatosis and cysticercosis were negative.

data.diagnosis: Subcutaneous dirofilariasis due to Dirofilaria repens
data.description: A zoonotic filarial nematode infection transmitted by mosquitoes, usually from dogs. Humans are accidental hosts and typically develop a solitary painless subcutaneous nodule containing an immature worm.
symptoms_in_common: Painless well-demarcated nodule in the upper arm
Exposure to a pet dog, an important reservoir host
Outdoor exposure in forested and island areas where mosquitoes may be present
Normal blood counts and inflammatory markers, which are common in localized human infection
Negative serology for other tissue helminths
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly atypical patient symptoms; localized painless nodules without systemic illness are typical

data.description: Infection with migrating larval tapeworms of Spirometra species, which can produce slowly migrating subcutaneous nodules after ingestion of contaminated water or exposure to infected amphibians or reptiles.
symptoms_in_common: Normal routine laboratory studies can occur in localized disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported ingestion of untreated water, frogs, snakes, or other potential intermediate hosts
Residence in Croatia is less typical than endemic regions of East and Southeast Asia
The histologic appearance is more suggestive of a filarial nematode than a cestode larva
Pet-dog exposure is more characteristic of Dirofilaria infection

data.description: Tissue infection with larval Taenia solium cysts. It may cause painless, mobile subcutaneous nodules, sometimes with associated neurocysticercosis.
symptoms_not_in_common: Migratory behavior of the nodules is not typical
Cysticercosis serology was negative
No exposure history suggesting ingestion of Taenia solium eggs was reported
No neurologic symptoms were reported
The lesion morphology shown is not typical of a cysticercus

data.description: A filarial infection caused by Loa loa, characterized by transient migrating subcutaneous swellings (Calabar swellings) and sometimes visible migration of worms across the eye.
symptoms_in_common: Localized lesions may occur without major systemic illness
symptoms_not_in_common: No travel to West or Central Africa, where Loa loa is endemic
No episodic angioedematous Calabar swellings were described
No eye symptoms or visible ocular worm migration
No eosinophilia was reported
Dog exposure and Mediterranean outdoor exposure favor Dirofilaria repens instead

data.description:
66-year-old man with progressive neurologic symptoms since around 2000, beginning with recurrent unexplained falls. In 2003 he developed blurred vision, photophobia, and worsening imbalance/unsteadiness. He had prior bilateral cataract surgery with lens implantation in 2000 without benefit. Symptoms gradually progressed to frequent falls requiring a cane, backward falling, retracted head, slurred speech, inability to look down, and dysphagia with repeated aspiration. 

On exam, pupils were irregular with sluggish bilateral light reflexes. Vertical voluntary gaze and smooth pursuit were slow and limited, with preserved vertical movements on passive head motion early on; horizontal gaze and pursuit were slow with bilateral adduction paresis and initially normal convergence. He later developed severe limitation of vertical and medial eye movements, absent convergence, absent Bell’s phenomenon, absent optokinetic and caloric nystagmus, and no doll’s eye response. He had severe nuchal rigidity, retrocollis, inability to sit unsupported, recurrent backward falls, axial rigidity, and slowed distal rapid alternating movements appearing ataxic. Reflexes were symmetric and minimally brisk with bilateral flexor plantar responses; no resting tremor was present.

A progressive tau-related neurodegenerative disorder characterized by early postural instability and falls, axial-predominant parkinsonism, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, dysarthria, dysphagia, and cognitive/behavioral changes.
symptoms_in_common: Early recurrent unexplained falls, particularly backward falls
Vertical voluntary gaze slowing and limitation, especially downgaze
Initially preserved vertical eye movements with passive head motion, consistent with supranuclear gaze palsy
Progressive loss of convergence and impaired vertical smooth pursuit
Progressive severe impairment of eye movements
symptoms_not_in_common: Irregular pupils with sluggish bilateral light reflexes
Bilateral adduction paresis early in the course
Initially normal convergence despite prominent horizontal adduction impairment
Marked photophobia and blurred vision as early prominent complaints
Absent caloric nystagmus and absent doll's eye response late in the course

data.diagnosis: Multiple system atrophy (MSA), parkinsonian or cerebellar phenotype
data.description: A rapidly progressive synucleinopathy causing autonomic failure with parkinsonism and/or cerebellar ataxia; eye movement abnormalities and dysphagia may occur, but a classic vertical supranuclear gaze palsy is less typical.
symptoms_in_common: Slowed rapid alternating movements that may appear ataxic
Abnormal smooth pursuit and slowed saccades
Lack of resting tremor can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Early recurrent backward falls as the presenting feature
Prominent vertical supranuclear gaze palsy with inability to look down
Preservation of vertical eye movement during passive head motion early on
Severe retrocollis
No autonomic failure described, such as orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention/incontinence, erectile dysfunction, or anhidrosis
Absent convergence and severe progressive ophthalmoplegia

data.description: A neurodegenerative tauopathy syndrome featuring asymmetric parkinsonism, limb apraxia, cortical sensory deficits, myoclonus, dystonia, and sometimes eye movement abnormalities or speech impairment.
symptoms_in_common: Possible impaired saccades and eye movement abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: Symptoms are predominantly axial rather than markedly asymmetric limb symptoms
No limb apraxia described
No cortical sensory loss described
No alien-limb phenomenon described
No myoclonus described
Early, marked vertical supranuclear gaze palsy and backward falls are more characteristic of PSP

data.diagnosis: Niemann-Pick disease type C, adult-onset form
data.description: A lysosomal lipid-storage disorder that can present in adulthood with vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, ataxia, dystonia, dysphagia, psychiatric symptoms, and progressive cognitive decline.
symptoms_in_common: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, particularly impaired downgaze
Initially preserved vestibulo-ocular/passive eye movements despite impaired voluntary vertical gaze
symptoms_not_in_common: Onset in later adulthood with a strongly PSP-like axial-rigid phenotype
Prominent early backward falls and retrocollis
No psychiatric syndrome, cognitive decline, hepatosplenomegaly, neonatal jaundice, or family history described
No cataplexy described
Severe axial rigidity is more suggestive of PSP

data.diagnosis: Whipple disease with oculomasticatory/oculofacioskeletal myorhythmia or CNS involvement
data.description: A rare infection caused by Tropheryma whipplei that may involve the central nervous system and cause eye movement abnormalities, ataxia, supranuclear gaze palsy, cognitive changes, and characteristic rhythmic facial or masticatory movements.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive eye movement abnormalities including vertical gaze impairment
symptoms_not_in_common: Very long, slowly progressive course over many years without systemic illness
No weight loss, diarrhea, abdominal pain, arthralgia, fever, or lymphadenopathy described
No cognitive or psychiatric symptoms described
No oculomasticatory, facial, or skeletal myorhythmia described
Prominent retrocollis and early backward falls are more typical of PSP

data.description: A 36-year-old man, sexually active with men, presented to the emergency department with a 2-week history of fever, headache, drowsiness, and photophobia. He was previously healthy. Physical examination revealed a temperature of 38.3°C and neck stiffness. CT of the head was normal. Lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 29 cm of water (ref: <20 cm). CSF analysis revealed: cell count 340 cells/µL (90% mononuclear cells, predominantly lymphocytes), glucose 46 mg/dL, and protein 0.80 g/L. HIV antibody test was positive with viral load 300,000 copies/mL and CD4+ count of 7 cells/µL.

data.diagnosis: Cryptococcal meningitis due to Cryptococcus neoformans
data.description: Opportunistic fungal meningitis caused by encapsulated Cryptococcus yeast, most commonly occurring in advanced HIV/AIDS. The images are consistent with encapsulated budding yeasts seen with India ink staining and mucicarmine staining.
symptoms_in_common: Subacute 2-week course of fever and headache
Advanced untreated HIV infection with CD4+ count of 7 cells/uL
symptoms_not_in_common: No symptoms are strongly atypical; fever and marked meningeal irritation can be less prominent in cryptococcal meningitis than in acute bacterial meningitis

data.description: A subacute or chronic meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, often producing lymphocytic CSF inflammation, elevated protein, low glucose, and increased intracranial pressure. It is more common in severe immunosuppression.
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF glucose is relatively preserved at 46 mg/dL rather than markedly low
No reported pulmonary tuberculosis symptoms, weight loss, night sweats, or cranial nerve palsies
CSF microscopy images show encapsulated yeasts rather than acid-fast bacilli

data.description: Inflammation of the meninges, sometimes with brain involvement, caused by viruses such as enteroviruses, herpes simplex virus, varicella-zoster virus, or HIV itself. CSF usually shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with normal glucose.
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly elevated opening pressure is less typical for uncomplicated viral meningitis
The 2-week progressive course and profound CD4+ depletion suggest an opportunistic infection
CSF protein is more elevated than is typical for many uncomplicated viral meningitis cases
CSF images demonstrate encapsulated yeast organisms rather than a viral cause

data.description: An acute infection of the meninges caused by bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae or Neisseria meningitidis, usually characterized by fever, headache, neck stiffness, altered mental status, neutrophilic CSF pleocytosis, high protein, and low CSF glucose.
symptoms_not_in_common: Two-week subacute presentation is less typical than the usual abrupt onset
CSF is predominantly lymphocytic rather than neutrophilic
CSF glucose is not markedly reduced
CSF images show encapsulated budding yeasts rather than bacteria

data.description: Central nervous system involvement by Treponema pallidum, which can cause aseptic meningitis, headache, cranial neuropathies, and lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis. Risk is increased among sexually active men with HIV.
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe immunosuppression with CD4+ count of 7 cells/uL more strongly supports an opportunistic infection
Markedly elevated opening pressure is less characteristic
No reported rash, genital lesion history, cranial neuropathies, or ocular symptoms
CSF images show encapsulated yeast organisms, not spirochetes

data.description: An 83-year-old woman presented to the acute stroke unit with sudden onset double vision that had lasted for three hours. She had a medical history of monoclonal gammopathy of uncertain significance and atrial fibrillation, for which she was not receiving anticoagulation because of an adverse reaction to warfarin. She had no history of transient ischaemic attack or stroke. She had diplopia only when looking through her right eye. On examination, she was unable to adduct her left eye, with nystagmus in her right eye when she attempted to do this. Her neurological examination was otherwise normal.

data.diagnosis: Acute ischemic infarction of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus (internuclear ophthalmoplegia due to pontine stroke)
data.description: A small ischemic stroke affecting the medial longitudinal fasciculus in the pons disrupts coordination between the abducens and oculomotor nuclei, producing internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
symptoms_in_common: Inability to adduct the left eye
Nystagmus of the right eye during attempted rightward gaze
Atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation, increasing embolic stroke risk
MRI appearance consistent with a small acute pontine lesion
symptoms_not_in_common: Diplopia described as occurring only when looking through the right eye

data.description: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia is an eye-movement disorder caused by damage to the medial longitudinal fasciculus, characterized by impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye and abducting nystagmus of the opposite eye.
symptoms_in_common: Right-eye nystagmus on attempted gaze toward the right
symptoms_not_in_common: Sudden onset is not specific to internuclear ophthalmoplegia itself, although it is typical when caused by stroke
Diplopia described as occurring only when looking through the right eye

data.description: An ischemic stroke in the vertebrobasilar circulation can affect the pons or midbrain and produce isolated ocular motor abnormalities, including internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
symptoms_not_in_common: Absence of other common posterior-circulation symptoms such as vertigo, ataxia, dysarthria, weakness, numbness, or dysphagia

data.description: Multiple sclerosis can cause demyelination of the medial longitudinal fasciculus and is a classic cause of internuclear ophthalmoplegia, often with diplopia and impaired eye adduction.
symptoms_not_in_common: Age of 83 years is highly atypical for new-onset multiple sclerosis
Sudden onset over three hours favors vascular disease rather than demyelination
Atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation strongly favors an ischemic cause
No prior neurological episodes suggestive of demyelination
MRI lesion pattern is more consistent with acute infarction

data.description: 35-day-old male infant, born at 37.5 weeks as a fraternal twin by cesarean section for breech presentation, previously healthy and feeding breast milk and formula, presented with 2 days of worsening fussiness, pallor, fever, vomiting, mottled skin, tachycardia, and respiratory distress. On admission he was pale, listless, and fussy, with temperature 39.1°C, pulse 176/min, respiratory rate 68/min with retractions, oxygen saturation 97% on 1 L nasal cannula, a holosystolic-flow murmur, splenomegaly 2–3 cm below the costal margin, and mottled, slightly cool extremities. Urinalysis showed dark red cloudy urine with blood, protein, and granular casts. Labs showed severe anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated LDH and AST, elevated D-dimer, and peripheral blood smear with multiple ring forms in erythrocytes; CSF was clear with mild pleocytosis and Wright stain showed intraerythrocytic ring forms.

A tick-borne intraerythrocytic protozoal infection that can rarely be transmitted transplacentally or perinatally. It causes hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, and splenomegaly; blood smears may show ring forms and tetrads (Maltese-cross forms) within red cells.
symptoms_in_common: Elevated LDH and AST consistent with hemolysis
Dark red urine with blood and protein consistent with hemoglobinuria
Mottled cool extremities and tachycardia during severe illness
Multiple intraerythrocytic ring forms on peripheral smear
Multiple ring forms within a single erythrocyte
Intraerythrocytic organisms seen on CSF Wright stain
symptoms_not_in_common: Holosystolic-flow murmur, although this may be a benign flow murmur caused by severe anemia
Mild CSF pleocytosis, which is not a usual prominent feature of babesiosis

data.diagnosis: Congenital malaria, especially Plasmodium falciparum infection
data.description: Malaria is a protozoal infection of red blood cells that may be congenitally transmitted from mother to infant. P. falciparum can produce multiple delicate ring forms in individual erythrocytes and may cause severe hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, and critical illness.
symptoms_in_common: Intraerythrocytic ring forms on blood smear
Multiple ring forms in individual erythrocytes
symptoms_not_in_common: Very young age without a stated maternal malaria exposure or travel history
Intraerythrocytic organisms reported in CSF, which is unusual because malaria parasites are generally identified in peripheral blood rather than CSF
Granular urinary casts, which are not a characteristic diagnostic feature of malaria
Holosystolic-flow murmur, likely secondary to anemia rather than malaria itself

data.diagnosis: Neonatal bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation
data.description: Sepsis in a young infant can cause fever, lethargy, respiratory distress, poor perfusion, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, and multiorgan injury. Disseminated intravascular coagulation may cause elevated D-dimer and thrombocytopenia.
symptoms_in_common: Tachypnea with retractions and respiratory distress
Mottled, cool extremities suggesting poor perfusion
Urinary abnormalities that may occur with renal hypoperfusion or multiorgan dysfunction
symptoms_not_in_common: Multiple intraerythrocytic ring forms on peripheral blood smear
Ring forms within erythrocytes on CSF Wright stain
Marked hemolytic anemia with elevated LDH and dark red urine strongly suggesting an intraerythrocytic hemolytic infection
Splenomegaly is less typical in acute neonatal bacterial sepsis

data.description: 70-year-old man with history of Gleason 9 (4+5) adenocarcinoma treated with radical prostatectomy 10 years ago. Presented to primary care with rectal pain persisting for several weeks. Patient had lost 20 lbs over 3-4 weeks and complained of progressive fatigue, poor appetite, severe tenesmus, and rectal pain. Patient had been living independently on West Coast but relocated to East Coast to be closer to adult children.

data.diagnosis: Metastatic recurrent prostate adenocarcinoma with rectal involvement
data.description: Late recurrence of high-grade prostate cancer after prostatectomy, with metastatic spread to sites such as lung and liver and possible local pelvic/rectal invasion causing tenesmus and pain.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple pulmonary nodules on CT consistent with metastatic disease
Liver lesion on CT consistent with metastatic disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No typical urinary obstructive symptoms, hematuria, or bone pain were reported

data.diagnosis: Primary rectal adenocarcinoma with metastatic disease
data.description: Cancer arising in the rectum can cause painful defecation, tenesmus, weight loss, and fatigue; advanced disease may metastasize to the liver and lungs.
symptoms_in_common: Pelvic/rectal mass or abnormality on CT
symptoms_not_in_common: No rectal bleeding, change in stool caliber, constipation, diarrhea, or iron-deficiency anemia was reported
Prior high-grade prostate cancer makes recurrent prostate malignancy an important competing explanation

data.diagnosis: Pelvic metastatic malignancy causing rectal compression or invasion
data.description: Metastatic cancer in the pelvis, including recurrent prostate cancer or another pelvic malignancy, can compress or invade the rectum and produce severe tenesmus and rectal pain along with constitutional symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Lung nodules and liver lesion suggesting disseminated malignancy
symptoms_not_in_common: No urinary retention, dysuria, fecal incontinence, bowel obstruction, or lower-extremity edema was reported

data.description: 27-year-old man with 3 days of progressive proximal leg myalgias followed by acute inability to lift his legs or stand on the day of presentation, with arm weakness. For several months আগে he had insomnia, loose stools, ~5 kg weight loss, and hand tremors. He started an herbal stress supplement 4 days before presentation. On exam: bilateral conjunctival injection, fine hand tremor, hyperreflexia, and symmetric weakness (upper extremities 4/5, lower extremities 3/5). Labs showed severe hypokalemia (K 1.8 mmol/L), mild transaminitis, mildly elevated alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin, mild CK/aldolase elevation, and venous pH 7.29.

data.diagnosis: Thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis due to Graves disease
data.description: A potentially life-threatening complication of thyrotoxicosis in which potassium shifts into skeletal muscle cells, causing severe hypokalemia and acute flaccid weakness. Graves disease is supported by diffuse hypervascular thyroid imaging and lymphocytic thyroid pathology.
symptoms_in_common: Acute symmetric proximal leg weakness progressing to inability to stand
Possible precipitation after starting an herbal supplement
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral conjunctival injection is not a classic feature, although Graves orbitopathy can cause eye symptoms
Venous acidemia is not the usual acid-base pattern in pure potassium-shift thyrotoxic periodic paralysis

data.description: An autoimmune disorder in which thyroid-stimulating antibodies cause diffuse thyroid overactivity, often producing diffuse goiter, increased thyroid blood flow, tremor, weight loss, gastrointestinal hypermotility, and eye findings.
symptoms_in_common: Conjunctival injection or possible ocular involvement
Diffuse hypervascular appearance of the thyroid on ultrasound
Histologic lymphocytic thyroid infiltration compatible with autoimmune thyroid disease
Hypokalemic periodic paralysis as a recognized complication of thyrotoxicosis
symptoms_not_in_common: Abrupt severe paralysis is not typical of uncomplicated Graves disease and suggests thyrotoxic periodic paralysis
Prominent proximal leg myalgias are not a usual primary manifestation
Severe hypokalemia is not expected unless complicated by periodic paralysis or another potassium-losing process

data.diagnosis: Supplement-associated thyrotoxicosis or exacerbation of underlying Graves disease
data.description: Herbal or dietary supplements may contain thyroid hormone, iodine, stimulants, or other substances that can trigger or worsen thyrotoxicosis; in a patient with underlying Graves disease, this can precipitate thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.
symptoms_in_common: Onset of severe weakness shortly after beginning an herbal stress supplement
Severe hypokalemia with paralysis consistent with a thyrotoxic trigger
symptoms_not_in_common: The symptoms of weight loss, tremor, insomnia, and diarrhea began months before supplement exposure, suggesting pre-existing thyrotoxicosis rather than solely supplement-induced disease
Diffuse autoimmune thyroid histology would favor Graves disease over isolated exogenous thyroid hormone exposure
Conjunctival injection is not typical of simple supplement toxicity

data.description: An inherited skeletal-muscle channel disorder causing episodic weakness due to intracellular potassium shifts, often precipitated by carbohydrate intake, exercise, stress, or medications.
symptoms_in_common: Acute onset symmetric weakness predominantly affecting proximal lower limbs
Potential trigger from physiologic stress or a new supplement
symptoms_not_in_common: Weight loss
Loose stools
Insomnia
Fine hand tremor
Hyperreflexia
Conjunctival injection
Thyroid imaging and pathology findings suggestive of Graves disease
No reported family history or prior recurrent attacks

data.diagnosis: Hypokalemic weakness from gastrointestinal potassium loss
data.description: Diarrhea can cause potassium depletion and metabolic acidosis, leading to muscle weakness, cramps, and in severe cases paralysis.
symptoms_in_common: Venous pH of 7.29, which may be compatible with bicarbonate loss from diarrhea
symptoms_not_in_common: The diarrhea appears chronic and not described as severe enough to clearly explain potassium of 1.8 mmol/L
Fine tremor, weight loss, insomnia, and hyperreflexia point toward thyrotoxicosis
Acute periodic paralysis pattern is more characteristic of thyrotoxic hypokalemic periodic paralysis
Thyroid ultrasound and histology findings are not explained by gastrointestinal potassium loss
Conjunctival injection is not typical

data.description: A 70-year-old woman presented to the clinic for a routine examination. The patient reported that this mass had been present since birth. Her symptoms were minimal, with occasional difficulty cleaning the area and halitosis from entrapped food, but she was otherwise asymptomatic regarding the lesion.
A benign bony exostosis arising from the midline of the hard palate. It is usually asymptomatic, covered by normal mucosa, and may be lobulated or very large.
symptoms_in_common: Large midline palatal mass with a lobulated appearance
symptoms_not_in_common: Reported presence since birth, since tori more commonly become apparent later in life

data.description: A benign, slow-growing tumor composed of mature bone that can present as a painless, firm mass of the palate or other craniofacial bones.
symptoms_in_common: Potential food retention and difficulty with oral hygiene when large
symptoms_not_in_common: Presence since birth is less typical
A multilobulated broad midline palatal appearance is more characteristic of torus palatinus than an osteoma

data.description: A 52-year-old Korean man presented with a 1-month history of general weakness that was aggravated three days before his emergency room visit. Initial neurologic examination revealed disorientation of time, place, and person, attention deficit, immediate memory disturbance, dysarthria, weakness of bilateral upper extremities with increased deep tendon reflexes, and right hemiparetic gait. Blood work showed an elevated eosinophil count of 5,500/μL, representing 41% of total white blood cells. The patient's clinical history and basic examinations did not reveal any identifiable cause of hypereosinophilia, including parasitic infection, neoplasm, vasculitis, or allergy. Additionally, the patient had no prior clinical symptoms or signs suggesting Churg-Strauss syndrome, such as sinusitis or asthma. Cardiac enzymes were elevated with creatine kinase-MB at 7.3 ng/ml and troponin-I at 4.78 ng/ml. An echocardiogram revealed mild left ventricular inferior wall hypokinesia.

data.description: A 50-year-old man with a history of injecting drug use presented to the emergency department with reduced level of consciousness and left arm weakness following five days of swinging fever, rigors, and headache. His past medical history included hepatitis C infection, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and a recent hospital admission for discitis and psoas abscess. On examination, his temperature was 38.4°C but he was hemodynamically stable and alert. Physical findings included a soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border, splinter hemorrhages, a small digital infarct of the left third toe, and mild upper motor neuron pattern weakness in the left arm. data.description: 7-day-old female newborn born at full-term to a G1P1 mother with birth weight of 4,380 gm. Parents denied poor feeding, poor activity, or weak crying. On examination at Day 7, she had normal muscle power, normal reflex, no macroglossia, but slightly decreased facial folds. Newborn screening for Pompe disease showed GAA activity 0.18 uM/h (critical cutoff <0.5) and ratio 42.87 (critical cutoff acid β-glucosidase/GAA ≥20). Laboratory examination revealed elevated pro-BNP (8,738 pg/mL), CK (722 U/L), and ALT (112 U/L). Confirmatory testing showed deficient lymphocyte GAA activity (1.33 nmol/g pro/hr, normal mean 66.7). Patient did not have the common CRIM-positive Taiwan Pompe disease p.D645E variant. Mutation analysis revealed heterozygous c.2024_2026del (p.N675del) and c.2040+1G>T variants in trans.
