data.description: An inflammatory autoimmune myopathy characterized by proximal muscle weakness and characteristic photosensitive skin eruptions, often accompanied by elevated muscle enzymes and sometimes systemic manifestations.
symptoms_in_common: Mild AST and ALT elevation, which can occur with muscle inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Prayer sign and impaired wrist dorsiflexion are more suggestive of skin/fascial sclerosis than classic dermatomyositis
No specifically described heliotrope rash, Gottron papules, shawl sign, or proximal-predominant weakness
Prior allogeneic stem-cell transplantation strongly favors chronic GVHD as an alternative explanation
Alkaline phosphatase elevation is not a typical primary finding of dermatomyositis

data.description: A multisystem autoimmune disease that can cause photosensitive cutaneous eruptions, fever, musculoskeletal symptoms, positive ANA, and involvement of internal organs including the liver and kidneys.
symptoms_not_in_common: Male sex and age 41 are less typical demographic features for SLE
Prayer sign with reduced wrist mobility suggests sclerodermatous/fascial disease rather than lupus
No reported arthritis, oral ulcers, serositis, kidney disease, cytopenias, or neurologic manifestations
History of allogeneic transplantation makes chronic GVHD a more likely unifying cause

data.description: An autoimmune connective-tissue disease characterized by progressive skin thickening and fibrosis, reduced joint mobility, and potential internal-organ involvement. Skin sclerosis can produce a prayer sign.
symptoms_in_common: Impaired wrist dorsiflexion and prayer sign
Possible skin tightening/thickening suggested by the hand findings
Mild liver-enzyme abnormalities can occur in autoimmune overlap syndromes
Muscle pain and weakness may occur in scleroderma-myositis overlap
symptoms_not_in_common: Acute photosensitive rash after sun exposure is not a classic systemic-sclerosis presentation
Intermittent fever is not typical
No reported Raynaud phenomenon, sclerodactyly, digital ulcers, telangiectasias, dysphagia, or pulmonary symptoms
The post-transplant setting more strongly supports sclerodermatous chronic GVHD, which can mimic systemic sclerosis

data.description: 51-year-old Caucasian male patient with terminal kidney disease presenting with a 10-month history of pruritic papules on sun-exposed areas of extremities. Patient suffered from severe pruritus with impaired sleep. Medical history includes arterial hypertension, hyperuricemia, coronary heart disease, terminal kidney disease due to idiopathic nephropathy, kidney transplants in 1990 and 2001 with rejections in 2000 and 2007, peritoneal dialysis from 2007-2017, ongoing hemodialysis since 2017, and factor V Leiden mutation. No history of habitual UV-light exposure or carcinogen exposure. Medications included felodipine, bisoprolol, clonidine, ramipril, urapidil, cholecalciferol, acetylsalicylic acid, allopurinol, phenprocoumon, thyroxine, iodine, fluvastatin, calcium acetate, omeprazole, and sevelamer carbonate.

A disorder characterized by the recurrent eruption of multiple rapidly growing keratotic papules or nodules, often with a central keratin-filled crater. Keratoacanthomas are considered part of the squamous-cell carcinoma spectrum and may occur more frequently in immunologically altered patients.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple papules and nodules on sun-exposed extremities
Crusted or keratotic crateriform lesions visible on the hands and forearms
Progressive appearance of additional lesions over months
History of renal transplantation and prolonged dialysis, which may contribute to immune dysregulation
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe generalized pruritus with sleep impairment is not a defining feature of keratoacanthomas
No reported rapid spontaneous regression of individual lesions
No known family history or early-life onset described

data.description: A rare variant of eruptive keratoacanthoma characterized by numerous disseminated small keratotic papules, often on sun-exposed skin, with severe itching and recurrent crops of lesions.
symptoms_in_common: Predominantly sun-exposed distribution on the extremities
Long, progressive course with new lesions appearing over time
symptoms_not_in_common: The patient has a relatively localized extremity distribution rather than widespread generalized eruption
No facial predominance, ectropion, or extensive mucosal involvement reported
Lesion number appears lower than the hundreds to thousands often described in classic Grzybowski disease
Age of onset at 50 years is later than commonly reported

data.description: An inherited condition causing recurrent multiple keratoacanthoma-like squamous tumors that typically grow rapidly and then involute, often leaving scars.
symptoms_in_common: Scarring or post-inflammatory skin changes visible during the course
Histology compatible with keratoacanthoma in multiple excised lesions
symptoms_not_in_common: No family history of similar lesions is provided
No childhood or young-adult onset reported
No clear spontaneous regression of untreated lesions is described
The severe renal disease and dialysis history suggest an acquired rather than inherited predisposition

data.description: A keratinocyte skin cancer that may present as a rapidly growing hyperkeratotic, crusted, or ulcerated papule or nodule. Keratoacanthoma-type lesions can be difficult to distinguish histologically and clinically from conventional cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.
symptoms_in_common: Multiple persistent keratotic and crusted nodules on sun-exposed skin
Ulcerated or eroded lesions on the hands and forearms
Histology showing keratoacanthomas, which lie on the squamous neoplasia spectrum
Previous renal transplantation and chronic immune dysregulation, both associated with increased squamous neoplasia risk
Partial control with topical 5-fluorouracil and imiquimod, treatments used for superficial keratinocytic neoplasia
symptoms_not_in_common: The large number of simultaneous lesions is less typical of sporadic cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma
Severe pruritus is not a typical primary feature of squamous cell carcinoma
No metastases or lymphadenopathy were identified on computed tomography
No major ultraviolet exposure history is reported

data.diagnosis: Acquired perforating dermatosis associated with chronic renal failure and hemodialysis
data.description: A pruritic perforating skin disorder seen commonly in patients with diabetes or chronic kidney failure on dialysis. It causes excoriated hyperkeratotic papules and nodules, often on the extremities, due to transepidermal elimination of dermal material.
symptoms_in_common: Papular, crusted, excoriated lesions on the extremities
Possible trauma-related isomorphic response from scratching
symptoms_not_in_common: The lesions are concentrated on sun-exposed areas rather than the more typical extensor limbs and trunk distribution
Histology reportedly showed keratoacanthomas and verrucae rather than transepidermal elimination
The lesions have prominent keratoacanthoma-like crateriform tumor morphology
Treatment response to imiquimod and 5-fluorouracil favors keratinocytic proliferative lesions rather than perforating dermatosis

data.description: 15-year-old female with a history of ovarian cyst, initially presenting with left arm pain, frontal headaches, and conjunctival hyperaemia without fever or neurological deficits. Seven days later, she developed acute low back pain, left-sided paraesthesia, and left arm weakness. On admission she had mild left-sided weakness, proximal pain in the left arm and leg worsened by movement, no fever or meningism, and GCS 15. Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis and neutrophilia. By day 2, she developed dysuria, urinary retention, worsening left hemiparesis and pain, loss of temperature sensation below T2 on the left and T4 on the right, and bilateral Hoffman signs. CSF examination and electromyography were normal; PCR detected high Zika virus concentrations in serum, urine, and CSF, with other viral, bacterial, and autoimmune tests negative.

Acute inflammatory injury of the spinal cord caused by Zika virus infection, producing motor weakness, sensory deficits with a spinal sensory level, pain, and autonomic dysfunction such as urinary retention.
symptoms_in_common: Left arm and leg pain worsened by movement
Loss of temperature sensation below thoracic sensory levels
Bilateral Hoffman signs indicating upper motor neuron involvement
Normal electromyography, supporting a central rather than peripheral process
Zika virus PCR positive in serum, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid
MRI appearance consistent with spinal cord inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Conjunctival hyperaemia is more typical of the preceding systemic Zika infection than of myelitis itself
Frontal headaches are nonspecific and not a core myelitis manifestation
Leukocytosis and neutrophilia are not typical defining findings of viral myelitis

data.description: A syndrome of acute spinal cord inflammation causing bilateral or asymmetric weakness, sensory impairment below a spinal level, pain, and bladder or bowel dysfunction. It may be post-infectious, autoimmune, or infection-associated.
symptoms_in_common: Defined loss of temperature sensation below thoracic levels
Spinal MRI abnormalities suggestive of cord inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Conjunctival hyperaemia
Initial isolated left arm pain before clear spinal symptoms
High concentrations of Zika virus detected in serum, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid are not typical of idiopathic transverse myelitis

data.description: A severe form of transverse myelitis involving a long segment of the spinal cord, often associated with viral infection, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, or other inflammatory conditions.
symptoms_in_common: Asymmetric sensory deficits with thoracic sensory levels
Upper motor neuron signs including bilateral Hoffman signs
Cervical and thoracic spinal cord involvement on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: Conjunctival hyperaemia
Frontal headache without meningism
Leukocytosis and neutrophilia are nonspecific rather than characteristic

data.description: An autoimmune inflammatory disorder that can cause longitudinally extensive myelitis and optic neuritis. It is usually associated with aquaporin-4 or myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibodies, though antibody-negative cases occur.
symptoms_in_common: Sensory level involving loss of temperature sensation
Severe neuropathic or radicular limb pain
Possible longitudinal spinal cord lesion on MRI
symptoms_not_in_common: No visual loss, optic neuritis, or eye pain was reported
Conjunctival hyperaemia is not optic neuritis
Zika virus PCR positivity in serum, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid favors an infectious cause
Negative autoimmune testing argues against an autoimmune demyelinating disorder
Preceding viral syndrome is more suggestive of infection-associated myelitis

data.description: A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the central nervous system that can cause focal weakness, sensory symptoms, myelitis, and bladder dysfunction, typically with episodes separated in time and lesions disseminated in the brain and spinal cord.
symptoms_not_in_common: Very acute painful spinal syndrome with a thoracic sensory level is less typical than a focal partial myelitis
High Zika viral load in serum, urine, and cerebrospinal fluid favors Zika-associated myelitis
No prior neurologic episodes or evidence of dissemination in time was described
No typical brain, optic nerve, or multifocal demyelinating symptoms were reported
Conjunctival hyperaemia and systemic viral symptoms are not typical of multiple sclerosis

data.description: An acute immune-mediated peripheral polyradiculoneuropathy, sometimes triggered by Zika virus, that usually causes progressive symmetric flaccid weakness, reduced reflexes, and variable sensory symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Autonomic symptoms including urinary dysfunction can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral Hoffman signs suggest central upper motor neuron involvement rather than peripheral neuropathy
A clear thoracic sensory level is not typical of Guillain-Barre syndrome
Left hemiparesis/asymmetric weakness is less typical than symmetric ascending weakness
Normal electromyography argues against Guillain-Barre syndrome
Spinal cord MRI abnormalities support myelitis rather than peripheral nerve disease
Urinary retention early in the course is more characteristic of spinal cord involvement

data.description: 27-year-old male presented with headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting for 3 days before admission. Physical examination showed no palpable lymph-node enlargement or hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory findings showed: WBC count 49.5×109/L, hemoglobin 161 g/L, platelet count 36×109/L, with 95% blasts in peripheral blood smear. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was markedly elevated to 13,022 IU/L. Flow cytometry showed leukemic blasts were positive for CD2, CD7, CD5, and CD3, and negative for TdT, CD34, CD13, CD33, CD10, CD19, CD20, and CD22.

data.diagnosis: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (T-ALL/LBL), likely with TCRAD-associated rearrangement
data.description: An aggressive precursor T-cell neoplasm involving bone marrow and blood, commonly presenting with circulating blasts, cytopenias, high LDH, and sometimes leukostasis or central nervous system symptoms. T-cell markers are expressed, although some cases lack TdT and CD34.
symptoms_in_common: Headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting, which may reflect hyperleukocytosis/leukostasis or CNS involvement
Blasts positive for T-cell markers CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7
Absence of B-cell markers CD10, CD19, CD20, and CD22
Absence of myeloid markers CD13 and CD33
TCRAD-region chromosomal rearrangement shown by cytogenetic/FISH studies
symptoms_not_in_common: No mediastinal mass was reported
No lymph-node enlargement
No hepatosplenomegaly
TdT negativity, which is less typical for conventional T-ALL

data.description: A mature post-thymic T-cell leukemia characterized by marked lymphocytosis and expression of mature T-cell antigens, usually CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7. It most often affects older adults and commonly causes splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and skin involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Expression of mature T-cell antigens CD2, surface/cytoplasmic CD3, CD5, and CD7
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 27 years; T-PLL usually occurs in much older adults
95% blasts rather than typical prolymphocytes
Severe thrombocytopenia at presentation
No hepatosplenomegaly
No palpable lymph-node enlargement
Headache, dizziness, nausea, and vomiting are not typical presenting features
The reported TCRAD-associated cytogenetic abnormality is more supportive of a T-cell precursor neoplasm than classic T-PLL-associated abnormalities

data.description: A mature peripheral T-cell malignancy caused by human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1). Acute ATLL can present with leukemic blood involvement, high LDH, cytopenias, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, skin lesions, and hypercalcemia.
symptoms_in_common: Leukocytosis with circulating malignant T cells
Expression of mature T-cell markers CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7
Thrombocytopenia can occur in advanced leukemic disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Young age; ATLL generally occurs in adults after a long latency following HTLV-1 infection
No HTLV-1 infection status or epidemiologic risk was provided
No lymphadenopathy
No hepatosplenomegaly
No hypercalcemia was reported
No skin lesions were reported
CD7 is often reduced or absent in ATLL, whereas this patient's blasts are CD7 positive
Predominance of blasts is less typical than the characteristic pleomorphic 'flower cell' morphology of ATLL

data.diagnosis: Early T-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ETP-ALL)
data.description: A high-risk immunophenotypic subtype of T-ALL arising from very immature thymic T-cell precursors. It typically lacks CD1a and CD8, has weak or absent CD5, and often expresses stem-cell or myeloid markers such as CD34, CD117, CD13, or CD33.
symptoms_in_common: Acute leukemia presentation in a young adult
Marked leukocytosis with numerous circulating blasts
Expression of T-cell-associated markers CD2, CD3, CD5, and CD7
symptoms_not_in_common: Strong CD5 positivity, whereas ETP-ALL often has weak or absent CD5
No reported stem-cell marker expression; CD34 is negative
No myeloid marker expression; CD13 and CD33 are negative
TdT negativity is less typical for ETP-ALL
No reported CD1a, CD8, CD117, or HLA-DR results to support the ETP phenotype

data.description: 36-year-old Chinese man with a 1-month history of persistent fever. Previously healthy, with no significant past medical history, no prior TB, chronic illness, liver or kidney disease, transfusions, malignancy, or immune disease; not on regular medications and no travel abroad. On admission he was acutely ill with tachycardia, hypotension, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and bilateral pulmonary rales. He had persistent fever with pancytopenia, marked hyperferritinemia, and acute respiratory failure. Labs on day 1 showed leukopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen, and ferritin 375,554 ng/mL.

A life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by uncontrolled activation of macrophages and lymphocytes, producing cytokine storm, hemophagocytosis, cytopenias, hypofibrinogenemia, and extreme hyperferritinemia.
symptoms_in_common: Pancytopenia including leukopenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia
Critical illness with hypotension and tachycardia
Hepatosplenic enlargement suggested by abdominal imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No known prior immune disease or malignancy, although secondary HLH can occur in previously healthy individuals

data.description: Secondary HLH triggered by active Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, often disseminated or severe pulmonary tuberculosis. It may cause prolonged fever, lung infiltrates, hepatosplenomegaly, marrow hemophagocytosis, cytopenias, and very high ferritin.
symptoms_in_common: Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates/consolidation on chest imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: No documented prior tuberculosis
No stated chronic cough, sputum production, hemoptysis, weight loss, or known tuberculosis exposure
No reported travel abroad

data.description: Widespread infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis involving multiple organs, potentially including lungs, liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Disseminated TB can precipitate HLH and severe respiratory failure.
symptoms_in_common: Pancytopenia, which can occur with bone-marrow involvement or secondary HLH
symptoms_not_in_common: No prior tuberculosis history
No reported chronic respiratory symptoms before the acute deterioration
No stated weight loss, night sweats, lymphadenopathy, or known TB contact
Extreme ferritin elevation and hypofibrinogenemia are more characteristic of associated HLH than uncomplicated TB alone

data.description: A common infection-associated form of secondary HLH caused by EBV-driven immune activation. It frequently presents with persistent fever, cytopenias, liver/spleen enlargement, coagulopathy, and markedly elevated ferritin.
symptoms_in_common: Hypotension and severe systemic inflammatory illness
symptoms_not_in_common: Prominent bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and severe acute respiratory failure are less typical as the primary presentation
No reported sore throat, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis, or infectious mononucleosis-like illness
No EBV testing result is provided

data.diagnosis: Severe bacterial sepsis with disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
data.description: A severe systemic infection can cause shock, acute respiratory distress syndrome, thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen, and multiorgan dysfunction. Sepsis can also overlap with or trigger secondary HLH.
symptoms_not_in_common: Ferritin of 375,554 ng/mL is far more suggestive of HLH than routine bacterial sepsis
Pancytopenia affecting all three blood cell lines is less typical of uncomplicated sepsis
Bone-marrow hemophagocytosis supports HLH rather than isolated sepsis/DIC
One-month persistent fever is longer than typical untreated acute bacterial sepsis

data.description: An 81-year-old man presented to the ICU 10 days after a 4-week cruise in New Caledonia, Vanuatu, the Solomon Islands, and New Zealand. He was reported to have been in perfect health during the cruise. On examination, he was febrile (39.1°C) and comatose with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 6. He exhibited hemiplegia of the left side, paresis of the right upper limb, normal tendon reflexes, and a Babinski sign on the left side. A transient rash was observed within 48 hours of admission. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed leukocyte count of 41/mm³ (98% polymorphonuclear leukocytes), protein level of 76 mg/dL, and CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.75.
A mosquito-borne flaviviral encephalitis acquired in endemic parts of Asia and the western Pacific, causing fever, altered consciousness, seizures, and focal neurologic deficits.
symptoms_in_common: Recent travel to western Pacific islands where mosquito-borne flaviviruses may occur
Focal neurologic deficits including hemiplegia and upper-limb paresis
Babinski sign indicating central nervous system involvement
CSF pleocytosis and elevated CSF protein
Brain imaging abnormalities compatible with encephalitis or ischemic injury
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF predominance of polymorphonuclear leukocytes is less typical than lymphocytic pleocytosis
Transient rash is not a classic feature
Normal tendon reflexes are less characteristic than extrapyramidal signs or movement disorders

data.diagnosis: Dengue encephalitis with cerebral vasculopathy or ischemic complications
data.description: Neurologic involvement from dengue virus infection can cause encephalitis, altered mental status, seizures, rash, and occasionally vascular complications such as ischemic stroke or cerebral venous thrombosis.
symptoms_in_common: Travel to tropical Pacific regions where dengue is endemic
Severe altered mental status progressing to coma
CSF pleocytosis with mildly elevated protein
Imaging findings suggestive of cerebral vascular or ischemic involvement
symptoms_not_in_common: No thrombocytopenia, bleeding manifestations, or plasma leakage are reported
CSF neutrophil predominance is not the usual dengue CSF pattern
The patient was reportedly completely well during the cruise, without a described preceding dengue-like febrile illness

data.description: A mosquito-borne flavivirus infection that may cause meningitis, encephalitis, acute flaccid paralysis, coma, and focal neurologic abnormalities, especially in older adults.
symptoms_in_common: Advanced age, which is a major risk factor for severe neuroinvasive disease
Transient rash can occur in West Nile fever
Potential neuroimaging abnormalities in severe encephalitis
symptoms_not_in_common: West Nile virus is not a common explanation for exposure during all listed Pacific destinations
Polymorphonuclear-predominant CSF is less typical later in the disease course
Hemiplegia with upper motor neuron signs is less characteristic than asymmetric flaccid paralysis or tremor

data.diagnosis: Varicella-zoster virus encephalitis with cerebral vasculopathy
data.description: Varicella-zoster virus can produce encephalitis and inflammatory vasculopathy involving cerebral arteries, leading to multifocal ischemic strokes, focal deficits, and altered consciousness; it may occur with or without a typical vesicular rash.
symptoms_in_common: Multifocal focal neurologic deficits including hemiplegia and contralateral upper-limb paresis
Imaging suggestive of cerebral ischemic or vascular abnormalities
symptoms_not_in_common: The rash is described as transient rather than typical painful vesicular shingles or chickenpox lesions
No history of recent zoster, chickenpox, or immunosuppression is provided
CSF neutrophil predominance is less typical than lymphocytic inflammation

data.diagnosis: Acute bacterial meningitis with meningovascular cerebral infarction
data.description: Bacterial meningitis can cause fever, coma, neutrophilic CSF inflammation, cerebral vasculitis, arterial thrombosis, and ischemic strokes with focal neurologic deficits.
symptoms_in_common: Focal neurologic deficits including hemiplegia and paresis
Possible cerebral vascular abnormalities and ischemic lesions on imaging
symptoms_not_in_common: CSF glucose ratio of 0.75 is relatively preserved and is less typical of pyogenic bacterial meningitis
CSF leukocyte count of 41 cells/mm³ is lower than commonly seen in untreated bacterial meningitis
Transient rash is not typical except in specific infections such as meningococcemia
No neck stiffness, purpura, or other meningeal signs are reported

data.description: 20-year-old man with Crohn’s disease diagnosed at age 10, previously treated with prolonged glucocorticoids and improved over the past 3 years on weekly adalimumab, presented with 3 weeks of sore throat, nonproductive cough, rhinorrhea, and chills. Two weeks before presentation, after backpacking travel to the northwestern United States, he developed cramping left calf pain that worsened over 2 days, with swelling extending from the calf to the foot and a purpuric/erythematous rash on the dorsum of both feet. He had a history of multiple similar self-limited upper respiratory episodes. On examination, he was uncomfortable due to left leg pain, with left ankle synovitis, intact nasal septum, and normal peripheral pulses.

An immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis characterized by IgA deposition, often triggered by an upper respiratory infection and presenting with palpable purpura, arthralgia or arthritis, gastrointestinal disease, and possible kidney involvement.
symptoms_in_common: Recent sore throat, cough, rhinorrhea, and chills preceding the rash
Purpuric erythematous rash involving both feet and lower legs
Acute painful swelling of the left calf, ankle, and foot
Skin biopsy appearance consistent with leukocytoclastic vasculitis and vascular IgA, C3, and fibrin deposition
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly unilateral calf swelling is less typical than symmetric lower-extremity purpura
Crohn's disease is not a classic primary feature, although it may coexist with or contribute to IgA-mediated disease

data.description: A small-vessel inflammatory vasculitis of the skin that causes palpable purpura, most often on dependent lower extremities; it can follow infection, medications, autoimmune disease, or inflammatory bowel disease.
symptoms_in_common: History of Crohn's disease, an inflammatory condition associated with secondary cutaneous vasculitis
Histologic appearance of small-vessel vasculitis with inflammatory cell infiltration and vessel-wall injury
symptoms_not_in_common: Ankle synovitis is not a defining feature of skin-limited leukocytoclastic vasculitis
The prominent IgA deposition suggests the more specific diagnosis of IgA vasculitis rather than nonspecific cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis
Nonproductive cough and rhinorrhea are likely a trigger rather than manifestations of the cutaneous vasculitis

data.description: A drug-induced small-vessel vasculitis that can occur during treatment with tumor necrosis factor-alpha inhibitors such as adalimumab, commonly producing palpable purpura and sometimes systemic immune-complex manifestations.
symptoms_in_common: Purpuric rash on the feet and lower legs
Painful swelling of the lower extremity
Arthritis or synovitis of the ankle
Biopsy findings compatible with immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis
symptoms_not_in_common: He had apparently tolerated adalimumab with clinical improvement for approximately 3 years before this episode
A recent upper respiratory illness provides an alternative and more immediate trigger
The specific vascular IgA deposition more strongly supports IgA vasculitis

data.description: An ANCA-associated necrotizing vasculitis involving small and medium vessels, classically causing chronic sinonasal disease, pulmonary symptoms, kidney disease, and sometimes purpura or arthritis.
symptoms_in_common: Sore throat and recurrent upper respiratory-type symptoms
symptoms_not_in_common: Nasal septum was intact, without destructive sinonasal disease
Rhinorrhea and sore throat were acute rather than chronic destructive upper-airway symptoms
No hemoptysis, dyspnea, pulmonary infiltrates, or renal manifestations were described
IgA-dominant immune-complex deposition is not typical of ANCA-associated granulomatosis with polyangiitis

data.diagnosis: Deep venous thrombosis of the left lower extremity
data.description: Formation of a blood clot in a deep leg vein causing acute unilateral calf pain and swelling; inflammatory bowel disease and recent travel can increase thrombotic risk.
symptoms_in_common: Progressive swelling extending from the calf to the foot
Crohn's disease, which increases venous thromboembolism risk
History of prolonged glucocorticoid exposure, a potential additional thrombotic risk factor
symptoms_not_in_common: Purpuric erythematous rash affecting both feet is not typical of uncomplicated deep venous thrombosis
Left ankle synovitis is not typical of deep venous thrombosis
Recent upper respiratory symptoms are not typical of deep venous thrombosis
Skin biopsy evidence of immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis would not be explained by deep venous thrombosis

data.description: A 47-year-old man presented to his primary care physician with a six-month history of left-sided sore throat, ipsilateral otalgia, and a six-week history of a left-sided neck mass. He had never smoked and drank less than 5 units of alcohol per week. On examination in the ENT clinic, a firm fixed lymph node was palpable in the upper anterior triangle.

data.diagnosis: HPV-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma with cervical lymph-node metastasis
data.description: A squamous cell cancer arising in the tonsil or base of tongue/oropharynx, often related to human papillomavirus (HPV). It commonly occurs in nonsmokers and may first present with a metastatic upper-neck lymph node.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent unilateral sore throat for six months
Firm fixed upper anterior cervical neck mass
Imaging appearance of an oropharyngeal mass with PET-avid cervical lymphadenopathy
No smoking history and low alcohol intake, which are compatible with HPV-associated disease

data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the oropharynx, including the tonsil or tongue base, that can spread to upper cervical lymph nodes. Traditional risk factors include tobacco and heavy alcohol exposure.
symptoms_in_common: Imaging evidence of a likely pharyngeal primary lesion and cervical nodal disease
symptoms_not_in_common: Never smoked
Low alcohol consumption

data.description: Lymphoma can involve Waldeyer's ring, including the palatine or lingual tonsils, and can cause a pharyngeal mass with cervical lymph-node enlargement.
symptoms_in_common: Neck mass due to cervical lymphadenopathy
Sore throat from possible oropharyngeal involvement
Imaging showing a pharyngeal-region mass and enlarged cervical node
symptoms_not_in_common: Ipsilateral referred otalgia
Firm fixed node, which is more suggestive of metastatic carcinoma than lymphoma
No reported constitutional symptoms such as fever, drenching night sweats, or unintentional weight loss

data.diagnosis: Chronic cervical lymphadenitis from head-and-neck infection
data.description: Reactive or infectious enlargement of cervical lymph nodes may occur with chronic tonsillitis, dental infection, tuberculosis, or other upper aerodigestive infections.
symptoms_in_common: Ear pain can accompany pharyngeal inflammation
symptoms_not_in_common: Six-month persistent unilateral symptoms
Firm fixed lymph node
Imaging evidence of a focal PET-avid oropharyngeal mass with suspicious nodal features
No reported fever, acute infectious symptoms, dental symptoms, or improvement over time

data.description: 72-year-old white woman with 10-year history of recurrent cystitis. No systemic symptoms. Physical exam showed slight anemia. Urine cultures were positive for Escherichia coli. No hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy detected by CT and ultrasound. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and subsequent biopsies were negative for both pathologic lymphoid infiltrate and Helicobacter pylori. Otolaryngologic examination and bone marrow biopsy were negative. Serology for hepatitis C virus and hepatitis B virus was negative. No monoclonal component found in serum protein electrophoresis.

data.diagnosis: Primary extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT lymphoma) of the urinary bladder
data.description: A rare indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in the bladder, often associated with chronic cystitis and persistent antigenic stimulation. It commonly remains localized and may lack systemic manifestations.
symptoms_in_common: Negative bone marrow biopsy, consistent with localized disease
symptoms_not_in_common: No clearly reported hematuria
No reported urinary frequency, urgency, dysuria, or pelvic pain

data.diagnosis: Chronic cystitis with reactive lymphoid follicular hyperplasia
data.description: Chronic inflammation of the bladder caused by recurrent infection can produce lymphoid aggregates and follicular cystitis, which may mimic lymphoma histologically or cystoscopically.
symptoms_in_common: Positive urine cultures for Escherichia coli
symptoms_not_in_common: Slight anemia is not a typical feature of uncomplicated chronic cystitis
The described dense atypical lymphoid infiltrate and molecular/cytogenetic abnormality suggested by the images would not be typical of purely reactive cystitis

data.diagnosis: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the urinary bladder
data.description: An aggressive B-cell lymphoma that can involve the bladder either as primary disease or as part of systemic lymphoma. It usually shows larger atypical lymphoid cells and often causes more rapidly progressive symptoms than MALT lymphoma.
symptoms_not_in_common: No constitutional symptoms such as fever, night sweats, or weight loss
No lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or bone marrow involvement
Very long history of recurrent cystitis favors MALT lymphoma over aggressive lymphoma
No reported rapidly progressive urinary symptoms, gross hematuria, or pelvic mass

data.diagnosis: Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder with prominent inflammatory infiltrate
data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the bladder that commonly occurs in older adults and may present with urinary symptoms or recurrent urinary tract infections. Histology would show malignant urothelial cells rather than a clonal lymphoid infiltrate.
symptoms_in_common: Recurrent urinary tract infections can coexist with bladder carcinoma
Slight anemia can occur in malignancy
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported gross or microscopic hematuria
No reported urinary obstruction, irritative voiding symptoms, or pelvic pain
No systemic evidence of advanced carcinoma
Histologic appearance of a predominant lymphoid infiltrate is not typical of urothelial carcinoma

data.description: 95-year-old woman admitted after a fall. Medical history includes Alzheimer's disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (on metformin). Laboratory findings showed elevated white cell count and C reactive protein levels. Urine culture revealed Klebsiella pneumoniae infection. Blood cultures were negative.
A fracture through the neck of the femur, commonly occurring after a fall in frail older adults with osteoporosis. The pelvic radiograph is concerning for a proximal left femoral neck fracture.
symptoms_in_common: Likely fragility-related bone injury after low-energy trauma
symptoms_not_in_common: Elevated white cell count
Elevated C-reactive protein

Negative blood cultures

data.diagnosis: Intertrochanteric fracture of the left femur
data.description: A fracture through the proximal femur between the greater and lesser trochanters, typically caused by a fall in elderly patients and sometimes difficult to distinguish from a femoral neck fracture on a single radiograph.
symptoms_not_in_common: Leukocytosis
Raised C-reactive protein
Klebsiella pneumoniae urinary infection
Negative blood cultures

data.description: A bacterial urinary tract infection caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae. Older adults, particularly those with diabetes and dementia, may present with nonspecific symptoms such as weakness, confusion, or falls rather than urinary complaints.
symptoms_in_common: Urine culture positive for Klebsiella pneumoniae
Fall, which can be a nonspecific presentation in older adults
symptoms_not_in_common: No urinary symptoms were reported
Blood cultures were negative, which argues against bloodstream infection but not against a urinary tract infection

data.description: 22-year-old athletic male presented with swelling and locking of the left knee. He had no recent trauma but had several football injuries as a child. Two years prior, he had experienced disabling knee pain.

data.diagnosis: Osteochondritis dissecans of the femoral condyle with a detached osteochondral fragment
data.description: A focal disorder of subchondral bone and overlying cartilage, usually affecting the medial femoral condyle in young active males. An unstable or detached fragment may become an intra-articular loose body and cause mechanical symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Previous episode of disabling knee pain
Radiographic appearance suggestive of an osteochondral fragment/loose body
symptoms_not_in_common: No recent trauma

data.description: A free fragment of bone and cartilage within the knee joint, commonly resulting from osteochondritis dissecans, prior osteochondral injury, or degenerative joint disease. It can intermittently obstruct joint movement.
symptoms_in_common: History of childhood football-related knee injuries
Visible ossified intra-articular fragment on radiographs
symptoms_not_in_common: No recent acute traumatic event
Young age is less typical when the loose body is caused by degenerative osteoarthritis

data.description: A benign proliferative disorder of synovium that forms cartilaginous nodules, which may calcify or ossify and detach into the joint as loose bodies. It commonly causes recurrent swelling, pain, and locking.
symptoms_in_common: Possible ossified intra-articular body on radiographs
symptoms_not_in_common: History of childhood sports injuries is not required or characteristic
Radiographs appear to show a limited number of fragments rather than the multiple similarly sized loose bodies more typical of synovial chondromatosis
No mention of chronic progressive pain or reduced range of motion

data.description: 48-year-old male presented with 1-week history of jaundice, dark brown urine, pale stools, and nausea. Medical history and physical exam were unremarkable. Laboratory findings showed hepatic panel in cholestatic pattern: total bilirubin 117 μmol/L, conjugated bilirubin 66.8 μmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 173 IU/L, γ-Glutamyltransferase 380 IU/L, Alanine transaminase 468 IU/L. CA19-9 was 11783 IU/mL. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and β2-microglobulin were normal.

data.diagnosis: Primary pancreatic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
data.description: A rare extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma arising in the pancreas, most often diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, which can form a pancreatic head mass and obstruct the bile duct.
symptoms_in_common: Absence of significant prior medical history or systemic symptoms can occur
symptoms_not_in_common: Markedly elevated CA19-9, which is more classically associated with pancreaticobiliary adenocarcinoma but may rise substantially from biliary obstruction
Normal LDH and beta-2-microglobulin, which can be elevated in aggressive lymphoma but may remain normal in localized disease

data.description: A malignant epithelial tumor of the pancreatic ducts, commonly arising in the pancreatic head and causing extrahepatic biliary obstruction.
symptoms_in_common: Pancreatic head-region mass with biliary obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 48 years, which is younger than the typical presentation age
Histologic appearance suggestive of a lymphoid rather than gland-forming epithelial neoplasm

data.description: Cancer of the distal extrahepatic bile duct that produces progressive obstruction of bile flow and may appear as a mass near the pancreatic head.
symptoms_not_in_common: Imaging centered on a pancreatic mass rather than a clearly bile-duct-centered lesion
Lymphoid histologic appearance rather than malignant biliary epithelial glands

data.description: An immune-mediated inflammatory pancreatic disorder, often related to IgG4 disease, that can enlarge the pancreatic head and mimic pancreatic cancer by compressing the distal common bile duct.
symptoms_in_common: Pancreatic enlargement or mass-like lesion causing biliary obstruction
symptoms_not_in_common: Extremely high CA19-9 level, although obstruction can elevate CA19-9
Tumor histology composed of atypical lymphoid cells rather than the characteristic lymphoplasmacytic inflammation and fibrosis of autoimmune pancreatitis
No reported history of other IgG4-related organ involvement

data.description: 80-year-old woman with 6-month history of slowly increasing asymptomatic lumbar subcutaneous mass. History of chronic renal failure requiring dialysis three times weekly for 10 years. Poor compliance with phosphate-binding medications and dietary restrictions. Physical exam showed firm, immobile subcutaneous nodule measuring 9 cm in major axis. Laboratory findings: serum calcium 1.95 mmol/L (normal: 2.05-2.55), serum phosphorus 3.3 mmol/L (normal: 0.74-1.52), serum intact parathyroid hormone 142 ng/L (normal: 10-65), serum creatinine 787 μmol/L (normal: 53-106).

data.diagnosis: Tumoral calcinosis secondary to chronic renal failure (uremic tumoral calcinosis)
data.description: Periarticular or subcutaneous deposition of calcium-phosphate material forming large, lobulated calcified masses, often occurring in long-term dialysis patients with hyperphosphatemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism.
symptoms_in_common: Slowly enlarging painless subcutaneous lumbar mass
Long-term hemodialysis for chronic renal failure
Elevated intact parathyroid hormone consistent with secondary hyperparathyroidism
Poor adherence to phosphate binders and dietary phosphate restriction
Imaging appearance of a large lobulated calcified periarticular/subcutaneous mass
symptoms_not_in_common: Hypocalcemia is less typical than normal or elevated calcium in some non-uremic forms, although it is compatible with dialysis-associated disease

data.diagnosis: Metastatic calcification due to calcium-phosphate imbalance in end-stage renal disease
data.description: Deposition of calcium salts in otherwise normal soft tissues due to systemic mineral metabolism abnormalities, particularly hyperphosphatemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism in renal failure.
symptoms_in_common: End-stage chronic renal failure requiring dialysis
symptoms_not_in_common: A single large, sharply mass-like 9 cm lesion is more characteristic of uremic tumoral calcinosis than diffuse metastatic calcification
Low serum calcium is not the classic biochemical pattern for metastatic calcification

data.description: Deposition of insoluble calcium salts in the skin or subcutaneous tissue. In this patient, a metabolic subtype related to renal failure and hyperphosphatemia would be most relevant.
symptoms_in_common: Abnormal calcium-phosphate metabolism from chronic renal failure
symptoms_not_in_common: The lesion is unusually large for common localized calcinosis cutis
There is no reported chalky discharge, ulceration, or overlying skin breakdown
No reported connective-tissue disease such as dermatomyositis or systemic sclerosis

data.diagnosis: Secondary hyperparathyroidism of chronic kidney disease with extraskeletal calcification
data.description: A chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder in which phosphate retention, impaired vitamin D activation, and hypocalcemia stimulate parathyroid hormone secretion, promoting bone and soft-tissue complications.
symptoms_in_common: Chronic renal failure treated with dialysis for 10 years
Soft-tissue calcified mass as an extraskeletal complication
symptoms_not_in_common: A discrete large lumbar mass is not a primary symptom of secondary hyperparathyroidism itself; it represents a complication such as tumoral calcinosis
No reported bone pain, fractures, pruritus, or skeletal deformities

data.description: A benign heterotopic bone-forming lesion in soft tissue, usually after trauma, surgery, neurologic injury, or repeated tissue injury; it may present as a firm enlarging mass with peripheral ossification.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported preceding trauma, surgery, or local injury
The patient has severe hyperphosphatemia and dialysis-associated mineral imbalance, favoring tumoral calcinosis
The lesion is subcutaneous and lobulated rather than a typical intramuscular zonal ossifying lesion
The mass is asymptomatic, whereas myositis ossificans may cause pain and restricted movement

data.description: 47-year-old female presented to emergency department after being hit while skiing by another skier at high speed from behind. Immediate pain and marked general swelling of the knee joint occurred after impact. Unable to bear weight. Physical exam showed neurovascularly intact limb with no broken skin. No relevant medical, family, or social history.

data.diagnosis: Lateral tibial plateau fracture (split-depression type, Schatzker II)
data.description: An intra-articular fracture of the lateral upper tibia involving a split component and depression of the articular surface; commonly occurs after high-energy valgus or axial loading trauma.
symptoms_in_common: Radiographic fracture involving the lateral tibial plateau

data.diagnosis: Tibial plateau fracture with associated hemarthrosis
data.description: A fracture extending into the knee joint can cause bleeding into the joint space, producing rapid swelling and painful limitation of weight bearing.
symptoms_in_common: Intra-articular proximal tibial fracture on radiographs

data.diagnosis: Anterior cruciate ligament injury associated with tibial plateau fracture
data.description: ACL tears can accompany high-energy tibial plateau fractures, particularly when the injury mechanism includes valgus stress, rotation, or anterior translation of the tibia.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported knee instability or giving-way sensation
Radiographs demonstrate a bony tibial plateau fracture, which is not required for an isolated ACL injury

data.diagnosis: Meniscal injury associated with lateral tibial plateau fracture
data.description: Lateral meniscal tears are frequently associated with lateral tibial plateau fractures because the meniscus can be trapped or injured by depression and displacement of the articular surface.
symptoms_not_in_common: No reported locking, catching, or focal joint-line tenderness

data.description: A 52-year-old woman presented with complaints of anal pain, constipation, and tenesmus for 3 months before being referred to the hospital. There were no relevant prior illnesses. Rectal digital examination revealed a 6-cm smooth elastic mass on the rectal posterior left side 2 cm from the anal verge. Colonoscopy showed a rectal submucosal bulging. Computed tomography scan and magnetic resonance imaging confirmed the presence of a single 6-cm well-delimited mass, compressing and infiltrating the wall of the medium to low rectum.

A rare mesenchymal tumor of the gastrointestinal tract arising from interstitial cells of Cajal or related precursor cells. Rectal GISTs are commonly submucosal, composed of spindle cells, and often show KIT and/or DOG1 immunoreactivity with KIT or PDGFRA mutations.
symptoms_in_common: Well-delimited 6-cm mass in the medium-to-low rectum
Compression and infiltration of the rectal wall
Adult patient in the typical age range for GIST
symptoms_not_in_common: No gastrointestinal bleeding was reported
No systemic symptoms such as weight loss or fever were reported

data.description: A benign smooth-muscle tumor that can arise from the muscularis mucosae or muscularis propria of the rectum. It generally presents as a circumscribed submucosal mass and may cause obstructive symptoms when large.
symptoms_in_common: Anal/rectal pain due to mass effect
Spindle-cell morphology can resemble smooth-muscle tumor
symptoms_not_in_common: Infiltration of the rectal wall is less typical for a benign leiomyoma
A 6-cm lesion with progressive symptoms is relatively large for a benign leiomyoma

data.description: A malignant smooth-muscle tumor of the rectum. It can form a submucosal or intramural mass and may produce pain, constipation, tenesmus, bleeding, or obstructive symptoms.
symptoms_in_common: Large intramural or submucosal rectal mass
symptoms_not_in_common: The lesion is described as smooth, elastic, and well-delimited rather than overtly aggressive or irregular
No rectal bleeding, weight loss, or metastatic disease was reported

data.description: An uncommon usually benign peripheral nerve-sheath tumor arising in the gastrointestinal wall. Rectal schwannomas are generally slow-growing, well-circumscribed submucosal masses that can cause obstructive symptoms.
symptoms_not_in_common: Rectal-wall infiltration is less characteristic of a typical benign schwannoma
A 6-cm low-rectal lesion is uncommon
The reported molecular and immunohistochemical pattern would be more suggestive of GIST than schwannoma if KIT/DOG1 positive

data.description: Ectopic endometrial tissue involving the rectovaginal septum or bowel wall, usually in women of reproductive age. It may cause rectal pain, constipation, tenesmus, and an infiltrative rectal-wall mass.
symptoms_not_in_common: Age 52 years is less typical, particularly if postmenopausal
No cyclic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, infertility, or menstrual association was reported
A solitary smooth 6-cm submucosal mass with spindle-cell tumor histology is less typical

data.description: Two-year-four-month-old female born at 39 weeks by Cesarean section for placental failure, with intrauterine growth restriction at birth (1850 g, 3rd percentile; length 44.5 cm, 3rd percentile; head circumference 31 cm, 3rd percentile). At 3 months, she was found to have bilateral severe sensorineural hearing loss and received hearing aids at 4 months. She has persistent short stature and low weight, with normal psychomotor development (sat at 8 months, walked at 14 months, talked at 13 months). Reported physical features include triangular face, prominent forehead, small chin, hypoplastic nasal alae, large mouth with thin downturned lips, low-set ears, deeply set eyes, delayed teething, microdontia, delayed bone age, thin wrinkled skin with visible vessels, and lipoatrophy. Brain MRI was normal. Genetic testing showed a de novo heterozygous PIK3R1 variant c.1956dupT (p.Lys653*).

A rare autosomal dominant developmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in PIK3R1. SHORT stands for short stature, hyperextensibility/hernia, ocular depression, Rieger anomaly, and teething delay; affected individuals often have intrauterine growth restriction, characteristic triangular facial appearance, lipoatrophy, thin skin, and delayed bone age.
symptoms_in_common: Persistent short stature and low weight
Large mouth with thin downturned lips
Thin wrinkled skin with visible vessels
symptoms_not_in_common: Bilateral severe congenital sensorineural hearing loss is not a classic core feature, although it has been reported in some affected individuals

data.description: A growth-restriction syndrome usually caused by abnormal imprinting at chromosome 11p15 or maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7. It is characterized by prenatal and postnatal growth failure, relative macrocephaly, triangular face, prominent forehead, feeding difficulty, and body asymmetry in some children.
symptoms_in_common: Birth weight, length, and head circumference near the third percentile
Persistent short stature and low weight
symptoms_not_in_common: Lipoatrophy
Thin wrinkled skin with prominent visible vessels
Hypoplastic nasal alae
Large mouth with thin downturned lips
Microdontia and marked delayed teething
Bilateral severe sensorineural hearing loss
De novo pathogenic PIK3R1 variant

data.description: A rare DNA-repair disorder, usually caused by biallelic ERCC6 or ERCC8 variants, with postnatal growth failure, progressive neurologic impairment, photosensitivity, cachectic appearance, retinal disease, and sensorineural hearing loss.
symptoms_in_common: Thin skin and reduced subcutaneous fat
symptoms_not_in_common: Normal psychomotor development
Normal brain MRI
No reported developmental regression or progressive neurologic deterioration
No reported photosensitivity
No reported retinal disease or visual impairment
Congenital intrauterine growth restriction is less characteristic than postnatal growth failure
De novo heterozygous PIK3R1 variant rather than biallelic DNA-repair gene variants

data.description: A group of genetic disorders characterized by near-complete lack of adipose tissue from birth or early infancy, resulting in a muscular appearance, prominent veins, hepatomegaly, insulin resistance, hypertriglyceridemia, and sometimes growth abnormalities.
symptoms_in_common: Low body weight and paucity of subcutaneous fat
symptoms_not_in_common: Severe intrauterine growth restriction is not typical
Triangular face with characteristic SHORT-syndrome facial features
Delayed teething and microdontia
Delayed bone age
Bilateral severe sensorineural hearing loss
No reported hepatomegaly, hypertriglyceridemia, insulin resistance, or diabetes
De novo heterozygous PIK3R1 variant
